0.title: Hosea: How Can I Give You Up?
0.overview:
Hosea preached in the eighth century BC to the northern kingdom of Israel, in the days of King Jeroboam II and the kings who followed him. On the surface it was a prosperous time. Israel's borders were wide, its trade was rich and its religious festivals were crowded. But underneath, the nation was rotting. The people worshipped Baal, the Canaanite god they believed sent rain and harvests, and bowed before golden calves. The rich cheated the poor, the priests neglected God's law, and in Hosea's lifetime four of Israel's last six kings were murdered by the men who replaced them. In 722 BC Assyria destroyed Samaria and carried the people away. Hosea was one of God's last great warnings before the end.

What makes Hosea unforgettable is that God made the prophet's own marriage into his message. God told Hosea to marry Gomer, a woman who would be unfaithful to him (1:2). Their children were given names that preached judgment: Jezreel, No Mercy and Not My People. Gomer, it seems, left Hosea for another man, and God told him, Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods (3:1). Hosea bought his wife back and brought her home. Christians have understood the details of this marriage in different ways, but its meaning is plain. Israel's idolatry was adultery against a God who loved his people like a faithful husband, and his love would not let them go.

The book has two parts. Chapters 1-3 tell the story of Hosea's marriage and what it means. Chapters 4-14 gather his sermons to Israel. They move back and forth between terrible warnings and tender promises, and the promises always have the last word. The sermons are full of vivid pictures: a half-baked cake, a silly dove, a stubborn heifer, love that vanishes like morning dew, a people who sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind (8:7).

Two words sum up what God wanted from his people and did not find. The first is knowledge. My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge (4:6). Not mere information, but a personal knowing of God that shapes a whole life. The second is steadfast love, God's own faithful covenant love, which he wanted to see reflected in his people. For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (6:6). Jesus quoted that verse twice, as the ancient Greek translation had it, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice", to rebuke religion that keeps the rituals and forgets the heart (Matt 9:13; 12:7).

Hosea shows us the heart of God more openly than almost any book in the Old Testament. God is a betrayed husband who says, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her (2:14). He is a father who taught his son to walk and bent down to feed him (11:3-4). And at the lowest point of the book, after every charge has been read, God cries out: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? ... My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (11:8). His judgment is real, and Hosea does not soften it. But his love is greater still.

The book is also a call to return. The word appears again and again. Israel would not return to God, so it would be carried away. Yet the book ends with an invitation and a promise. Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God (14:1). Take with you words, God says, and he gives the words of confession himself. And to those who return he promises, I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them (14:4).

Hosea points to Jesus Christ at every turn. Hosea bought back his unfaithful wife at a price. Christ bought his people not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19). God promised to betroth his people to himself forever, and Christ is the Bridegroom who loved the church and gave himself up for her (Eph 5:25). Matthew saw in the words out of Egypt I called my son (11:1) the story of Jesus, the true Son who lived out Israel's history without failing (Matt 2:15). Paul read the reversal of the names No Mercy and Not My People as the gospel reaching the Gentiles (Rom 9:25-26). And Hosea's cry, O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? (13:14), became Paul's shout of victory over death through the resurrection of Christ (1 Cor 15:55-57).

Some parts of Hosea are hard to read. Its language about sexual unfaithfulness is blunt, its pictures of judgment are violent, and God's command to Hosea is shocking. Faithful Christians differ on some questions: whether Gomer was already immoral when Hosea married her or became so later, whether the call to return in 6:1-3 was sincere or shallow, and whether 13:14 was first spoken as a threat or a promise. These notes explain the main views where they arise. But the bluntness is part of the message. God wants his people to feel how deeply sin wounds him, so that they may feel how astonishing his love is.

Hosea speaks to every believer whose love for God has grown cold, whose heart has wandered after other loves, or whose devotion has been like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away (6:4). It tells us that God knows exactly what we have done, that his judgment on sin is real, and that his love is stronger than our unfaithfulness. The book closes with a word for every reader: Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them; for the ways of the LORD are right (14:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word of the LORD comes to Hosea in the days of the kings of Judah from Uzziah to Hezekiah and of Jeroboam king of Israel (v. 1). God tells him, Go, take to yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people forsaking him is spiritual adultery, and God makes his prophet's own home the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word of the LORD that came to Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.

Hosea is the first of the twelve shorter prophetic books that close the Old Testament, often called the Minor Prophets. "Minor" refers to their length, not their importance.

The first verse sets the scene. After Solomon, God's people split into two kingdoms: Judah in the south, with its capital Jerusalem, and Israel in the north, with its capital Samaria. Hosea was a prophet to the northern kingdom. He began in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash (Jeroboam II), when Israel was prosperous and powerful. God had even allowed him to restore Israel's old borders (2 Kgs 14:25). But the prosperity hid a deep sickness. Jeroboam did what was evil in the sight of the LORD (2 Kgs 14:24), and the nation had largely turned to the worship of Baal and golden calves.

The list of Judah's kings, running to Hezekiah, shows that Hosea's ministry was long, stretching over several decades of the eighth century BC. He probably lived to see the northern kingdom collapse. In the years after Jeroboam's death, kings were murdered one after another, and in 722 BC Assyria captured Samaria and carried the people away. And this occurred because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God (2 Kgs 17:7). Hosea was one of God's last great warnings before the end.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, "Go, take to yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, "Go, take to yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD."

This is one of the most shocking commands God ever gave a prophet. The very first thing God tells Hosea to do is to marry a woman who will be sexually unfaithful.

Why? The verse gives the reason: for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD. God had bound himself to Israel in a covenant, like a husband to a wife. When Israel worshipped other gods, it was not a small religious mistake. It was adultery. Hosea's marriage would be a living picture of what Israel had done to God, and of what God felt about it. The prophet would not only preach God's message. He would live it, and feel it, in his own home.

Christians have understood this command in different ways. Some believe Gomer was already known for immorality when Hosea married her. Others believe she was faithful at first and became unfaithful later, and that the phrase a wife of whoredom describes her by what she would become, just as Israel was faithful for a time before it turned away. Some older interpreters thought the whole account was a vision or parable rather than a real marriage, because it seemed impossible that a holy God would command such a thing. But the book gives real names, real children and a real price paid (3:2), and most readers today take it as a real marriage. Either way, the point is the same. God's people had been unfaithful to him, and he wanted them to feel how deep the wound was.

Here is something we should not rush past. Hosea's marriage tells us that God is not a distant, unfeeling ruler. He loves his people like a faithful husband loves his wife, and he is grieved like a husband betrayed. Our sin is not only lawbreaking. It is unfaithfulness to a Person who loves us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–9 — Jezreel, No Mercy, Not My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hosea marries Gomer, and she bears a son named Jezreel, for God will punish the house of Jehu and end the kingdom of Israel (vv. 3-5). A daughter is named No Mercy, for God will no longer have mercy on Israel, though he will save Judah, not ... by bow or by sword (vv. 6-7). A second son is named Not My People: for you are not my people, and I am not your God (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Persistent unfaithfulness brings God's judgment, and the covenant relationship itself is put under threat.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went and took Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son. And the LORD said to him, "Call his name Jezreel, for in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel. And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he went and took Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son.

Hosea obeyed. He married Gomer. Notice the words bore him a son. With the next two children the text does not say "him" (vv. 6, 8), and some have wondered whether those children were Hosea's at all. We cannot be sure. But the names the children receive tell the story of a marriage, and a nation, coming apart.

And the LORD said to him, "Call his name Jezreel, for in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel.

The first child is named Jezreel, after a city and valley in northern Israel. The name carried a dark memory. Nearly a century earlier, a commander named Jehu had seized the throne and wiped out the family of wicked King Ahab at Jezreel in a bloodbath (2 Kgs 9-10). Jeroboam II, the king in Hosea's day, was Jehu's great-grandson.

This raises a question. God had commanded Jehu to judge Ahab's house (2 Kgs 9:7) and even commended him for doing it (2 Kgs 10:30). So why punish Jehu's family for the blood of Jezreel? The answer seems to be that Jehu did the right thing in the wrong spirit. He went far beyond what God commanded, killing for his own political advantage, and Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD... with all his heart (2 Kgs 10:31). God used Jehu's sword, but he did not approve Jehu's heart. It is possible to do God's work and still be under God's judgment for the way we do it.

The judgment came soon. Jeroboam's son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was assassinated (2 Kgs 15:8-10), ending Jehu's dynasty. Thirty years later the kingdom itself was gone.

And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel."

The valley of Jezreel was the great battlefield of northern Israel. The bow stands for Israel's military strength. All the power Jeroboam had built up would be broken.

verseByVerse.quote: She conceived again and bore a daughter. And the LORD said to him, "Call her name No Mercy, for I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel, to forgive them at all. But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the LORD their God. I will not save them by bow or by sword or by war or by horses or by horsemen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
She conceived again and bore a daughter. And the LORD said to him, "Call her name No Mercy, for I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel, to forgive them at all.

The second child is a daughter, and her name is terrible: No Mercy. The ESV notes that in Hebrew her name is "Lo-ruhama", which means "she has not received mercy". Imagine a father calling his little girl by that name every day. Every time Hosea called her, the people of Israel heard God's warning. God's patience, which had lasted for generations, was running out.

This is sobering. God is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, yet he will by no means clear the guilty (Exod 34:6-7). There comes a point when persistent, unrepentant sin meets the judgment it has been warned about.

But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the LORD their God. I will not save them by bow or by sword or by war or by horses or by horsemen."

Judah, the southern kingdom, would be spared for a time. And notice how. Not by armies: I will not save them by bow or by sword. That is exactly what happened in 701 BC, when the Assyrian army surrounded Jerusalem and the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians (2 Kgs 19:35). Jerusalem did not fire an arrow.

That is always how God saves. Not by human strength, but by the LORD their God. Our salvation does not depend on our resources but on his.

verseByVerse.quote: When she had weaned No Mercy, she conceived and bore a son. And the LORD said, "Call his name Not My People, for you are not my people, and I am not your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When she had weaned No Mercy, she conceived and bore a son.

Children were usually weaned at two or three years old. Time passes. Nothing changes in Israel.

And the LORD said, "Call his name Not My People, for you are not my people, and I am not your God."

The third name is the worst of all. Not My People, in Hebrew "Lo-ammi", as the ESV notes. At the heart of the covenant God had made with Israel was a promise: I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Now God speaks the reverse. You are not my people, and I am not your God. The ESV notes that the last phrase is literally "I am not yours". It is the language of divorce.

The three names form a downward staircase. Jezreel: judgment is coming. No Mercy: God's patience is ending. Not My People: the relationship itself is broken. This is where unfaithfulness finally leads. The greatest punishment is not suffering but separation from God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — Children of the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, and in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," it shall be said to them, "Children of the living God" (v. 10). Judah and Israel will be gathered under one head, for great shall be the day of Jezreel (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God's last word is not rejection but adoption, fulfilled in the gospel that makes outsiders God's children.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or numbered. And in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," it shall be said to them, "Children of the living God." And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head. And they shall go up from the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or numbered. And in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," it shall be said to them, "Children of the living God."

(The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible these last two verses begin chapter 2.)

And then, with no warning, comes the word Yet. Right after Not My People, God makes a promise that seems impossible. Israel will become as numerous as the sand of the sea, the very promise God made to Abraham (Gen 22:17). And in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," they will be called Children of the living God. (The ESV notes it may be "Sons".)

This is the rhythm of the whole book of Hosea, and of the whole Bible: judgment, and then grace that is greater than the judgment. God's last word to his people is not "Not mine" but "My children."

The New Testament tells us how far this promise reaches. Paul quotes this very verse and applies it to Gentiles, people who were never part of Israel, who are brought into God's family through Christ: And in the very place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they will be called 'sons of the living God' (Rom 9:26). Peter says the same to believers scattered across the Roman world: Once you were not a people, but now you are God's people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy (1 Pet 2:10). Every Christian was once "Not My People" and "No Mercy". In Christ, the names have been changed.

And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head. And they shall go up from the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel.

The divided kingdoms will be reunited under one head, one leader. Chapter 3 names him: David their king (3:5), the promised descendant of David. The prophets spoke of him as one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23). He is Jesus Christ, the Son of David, who gathers one people from every tribe and nation.

And great shall be the day of Jezreel. The name that meant judgment now means hope. The ESV notes at 2:22 that Jezreel means "God will sow". The valley where Israel's bow was broken will become the field where God sows his people again. God does not merely reverse judgment. He turns the very place of shame into the place of blessing.

1.title: Not My People
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Hosea in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. God tells him to take a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, because the land has committed great whoredom by forsaking the LORD (vv. 1-2).

Hosea marries Gomer, daughter of Diblaim. Their son is named Jezreel, for God will soon punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, end the kingdom of Israel and break Israel's bow in the Valley of Jezreel. A daughter is named No Mercy, for God will no longer have mercy on Israel, though he will have mercy on Judah and save them by himself, not by bow, sword or war. A second son is named Not My People, for they are not God's people and he is not their God (vv. 3-9).

Yet Israel will be as countless as the sand of the sea, and where it was said, "You are not my people," they will be called children of the living God. Judah and Israel will be gathered together under one head, for great will be the day of Jezreel (vv. 10-11).
1.theology:
Idolatry is spiritual adultery against a God who loves his people as a husband loves his wife (v. 2; Isa 54:5; Jer 2:2).

God may use a person's actions while judging the spirit in which they were done (v. 4; 2 Kgs 10:30-31).

God is slow to anger but will not clear the guilty; persistent unfaithfulness ends in judgment and separation from God (vv. 4-9; Exod 34:6-7; 2 Kgs 17:6-7).

God saves by his own power, not by human strength (v. 7; 2 Kgs 19:35).

God's final word is grace greater than judgment: those who were not his people become children of the living God, a promise fulfilled as Jews and Gentiles are brought into God's family through Christ (v. 10; Rom 9:25-26; 1 Pet 2:10; Gen 22:17).

God's scattered people will be gathered under one head, the Son of David (v. 11; 3:5; Ezek 34:23-24).
1.examples:
A prophet told to marry a woman who will betray him.

A prosperous nation with a rotten heart.

A little girl named No Mercy.

A king who did God's work with the wrong heart.

A city saved without firing an arrow.

A name that sounds like divorce: Not My People.

A valley of judgment renamed "God will sow".

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Say to your brothers, "You are my people," and to your sisters, "You have received mercy." (v. 1). But first the children must plead with their mother to put away her whoring, or she will be stripped and left in the wilderness (vv. 2-5). She says, I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, so God will hedge up her way until she says, I will go and return to my first husband (vv. 5-7). She did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil; so God will take back his gifts, end her feasts and punish her for the days of the Baals when she forgot me (vv. 8-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry credits other lovers with God's gifts, and God lovingly takes those gifts away to bring his people back.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to your brothers, "You are my people," and to your sisters, "You have received mercy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Say to your brothers, "You are my people," and to your sisters, "You have received mercy."

This verse finishes the thought of 1:10-11. (The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible it is numbered 2:3.) The ESV also notes that the Hebrew words are "ammi", which means "my people", and "ruhama", which means "she has received mercy". The names of Hosea's children are changed. Lo-ammi, Not My People, becomes Ammi, My People. Lo-ruhama, No Mercy, becomes Ruhama, Mercy. God simply drops the "not".

That is what the gospel does. It does not polish our old identity. It reverses it. The chapter begins with the end of the story so that we can read the painful middle with hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "Plead with your mother, plead— for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband— that she put away her whoring from her face, and her adultery from between her breasts; lest I strip her naked and make her as in the day she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and make her like a parched land, and kill her with thirst. Upon her children also I will have no mercy, because they are children of whoredom. For their mother has played the whore; she who conceived them has acted shamefully. For she said, 'I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Plead with your mother, plead— for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband— that she put away her whoring from her face, and her adultery from between her breasts;

Now we go back to the heartbreak. The scene is like a family court. The husband calls on the children to plead with their mother. On one level this is Hosea's family. On a deeper level it is God speaking to Israel. The mother is the nation as a whole, and the children are its individual people. God is calling the faithful few to plead with the nation to repent.

For she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. The relationship is broken. Yet notice the goal of the whole speech: that she put away her whoring. The husband is not seeking a way out. He is seeking her return.

lest I strip her naked and make her as in the day she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and make her like a parched land, and kill her with thirst.

If she will not turn, she will be stripped of everything. In ancient Israel a husband provided his wife's clothing. To strip her was to take back all he had given and leave her as poor and exposed as the day she was born. Ezekiel used the same picture: God found Israel as an abandoned baby, clothed her, made her his bride, and she used his gifts to play the harlot (Ezek 16:8, 15). The land itself would become a parched land, a terrible threat to people who were worshipping Baal precisely because they thought he gave rain.

Upon her children also I will have no mercy, because they are children of whoredom.

For their mother has played the whore; she who conceived them has acted shamefully. For she said, 'I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.'

Here is the heart of Israel's sin. Who were the lovers? The Baals, the Canaanite gods of storm and fertility. The people believed that Baal sent the rain and made the crops grow. So, to be sure of a good harvest, they served Baal. It was practical religion: worship whichever god seems to deliver the goods.

Listen to what she says her lovers give her: bread... water... wool... flax... oil... drink. Food, clothing and comfort. Her religion was about getting things. She did not love her lovers. She loved what they gave her.

That is the root of idolatry in every age. An idol is anything we look to for the things only God can give: security, meaning, pleasure, approval. Money, career, relationships, success. We go after them because we believe they will give me my bread.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, so that she cannot find her paths. She shall pursue her lovers but not overtake them, and she shall seek them but shall not find them. Then she shall say, 'I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now.' And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, so that she cannot find her paths.

Here is a surprising kind of judgment. God does not simply let her go. He blocks her road. He plants thorns in her path and builds a wall. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "your way", as God turns to speak to her directly.)

This is mercy disguised as frustration. Sometimes God lets the things we chase fail, the relationships sour, the plans fall through, because he loves us too much to let us find happiness apart from him. Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67). For the Lord disciplines the one he loves (Heb 12:6).

She shall pursue her lovers but not overtake them, and she shall seek them but shall not find them. Then she shall say, 'I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now.'

Her lovers keep slipping out of reach, and finally she comes to her senses: it was better for me then than now. It is exactly what the prodigal son discovered in the far country, feeding pigs: How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! (Luke 15:17).

Her motive is not yet pure. She wants to go back because life was better. But God often begins there. Many people first turn to him because their idols have failed them. He receives them, and then he teaches them to love him for himself.

And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.

This is the saddest verse in the chapter. Every good thing she thought came from Baal had come from God all along. It was I who gave. He even lavished silver and gold on her, and she melted it down to make idols.

Moses had warned about this: Beware lest you say in your heart, 'My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.' You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth (Deut 8:17-18). Paul says of all humanity, although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him (Rom 1:21). Every meal, every paycheck and every breath is a gift from the God many people never thank. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above (Jas 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will take back my grain in its time, and my wine in its season, and I will take away my wool and my flax, which were to cover her nakedness. Now I will uncover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one shall rescue her out of my hand. And I will put an end to all her mirth, her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her appointed feasts. And I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees, of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers have given me.' I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall devour them. And I will punish her for the feast days of the Baals when she burned offerings to them and adorned herself with her ring and jewelry, and went after her lovers and forgot me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I will take back my grain in its time, and my wine in its season, and I will take away my wool and my flax, which were to cover her nakedness.

Notice the word my: my grain, my wine, my wool and my flax. God reclaims what was always his. If she will not see that the gifts come from him, he will show her by taking them away, in its time and in its season, just when she expects the harvest.

Now I will uncover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one shall rescue her out of my hand.

Her lovers will be shown to be powerless. They cannot protect her. No one shall rescue her out of my hand. Idols always abandon us at the moment we need them most.

And I will put an end to all her mirth, her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her appointed feasts.

Israel still kept the religious calendar that God had given: new moons, Sabbaths, appointed feasts. But they had mixed it with Baal worship, and God calls them her feasts, not his. Religious activity without faithfulness means nothing to God. He would put an end to it.

And I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees, of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers have given me.' I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall devour them.

She called her vineyards my wages, the payment a prostitute receives. That is how she saw her relationship with the gods: a transaction. God would let the vineyards grow wild, a forest for wild animals.

And I will punish her for the feast days of the Baals when she burned offerings to them and adorned herself with her ring and jewelry, and went after her lovers and forgot me, declares the LORD.

The charge ends with two words that break the heart: forgot me. She dressed up in jewelry for her lovers, and she forgot the husband who loved her. That was Israel's deepest sin. Not only disobedience, but forgetfulness of God. It is still one of the most common sins among those who have known him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her, and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (vv. 14-15). She will call God My Husband, and the names of the Baals will be forgotten (vv. 16-17). God will make a covenant of peace (v. 18): And I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy (vv. 19-20). Heaven and earth will answer with blessing, and I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God' (vv. 21-23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to unfaithfulness is a new betrothal in which he himself provides everything the marriage needs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her. And there I will give her her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. And there she shall answer as in the days of her youth, as at the time when she came out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.

Now comes one of the most astonishing turns in the Bible. After verse 13, we expect: "Therefore I will destroy her." Instead God says, Therefore, behold, I will allure her. The same word Therefore that introduced judgment in verses 6 and 9 now introduces love. Her sin is the reason for his pursuit.

I will allure her. God will woo her again, like a young man courting. And bring her into the wilderness. The wilderness was where God first took Israel after the exodus, where he made his covenant with them and they were his bride. Jeremiah recalled it: I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness (Jer 2:2). There, stripped of Baal's vineyards, with nothing else to distract her, God will speak tenderly to her.

That is what God often does with his wandering people. He brings them into a wilderness, a season of loss or loneliness, not to destroy them but to speak to their hearts where they can finally hear him.

And there I will give her her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. And there she shall answer as in the days of her youth, as at the time when she came out of the land of Egypt.

God will give back the vineyards he took away, now received as gifts from him. And he will make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. The ESV notes that Achor means "trouble", and points to Joshua 7:26. The Valley of Achor was where Achan was stoned for stealing what God had devoted to destruction, just as Israel was entering the promised land (Josh 7:25-26). It was a place of sin, shame and death at the very doorway of the land.

God will turn that valley of trouble into a door of hope. The place where sin brought judgment will become the entrance to a new beginning. For the Christian, this is exactly what the cross is. The place of the worst trouble in history, where the Son of God bore the judgment for sin, has become the door of hope for all who come to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "And in that day, declares the LORD, you will call me 'My Husband,' and no longer will you call me 'My Baal.' For I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and they shall be remembered by name no more. And I will make for them a covenant on that day with the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the creeping things of the ground. And I will abolish the bow, the sword, and war from the land, and I will make you lie down in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And in that day, declares the LORD, you will call me 'My Husband,' and no longer will you call me 'My Baal.'

Israel had so mixed the worship of the LORD with the worship of Baal that they had begun to speak of God himself as their Baal. The names and the practices had blurred together. In that day, God says, the confusion will end. She will call him My Husband, a name of love and belonging, and never again confuse him with the idols.

For I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and they shall be remembered by name no more.

Notice that God himself does it: I will remove. We cannot cleanse our own hearts of their idols. God must take them away. That is what the new covenant promises: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer 31:33).

And I will make for them a covenant on that day with the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the creeping things of the ground. And I will abolish the bow, the sword, and war from the land, and I will make you lie down in safety.

In verse 12, God had threatened that wild beasts would devour her vineyards. Now he makes a covenant with the beasts for her sake. And he will abolish war. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says "break", the same idea as breaking Israel's bow in 1:5.) The restored bride will lie down in safety.

This looks beyond anything Israel experienced in history, to the peace of the new creation, where the wolf and the lamb shall graze together (Isa 65:25) and the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption (Rom 8:21). The restoration of God's people and the restoration of the world belong together.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy. I will betroth you to me in faithfulness. And you shall know the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy.

These are some of the most beautiful words God ever spoke. Three times he says, I will betroth you to me.

In ancient Israel, betrothal was more than an engagement. It was a binding commitment, and the bridegroom paid a bride-price to the bride's family. Here God names the bride-price he will pay: righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy and faithfulness. The bride brings nothing. The groom brings everything the marriage needs.

And it will be forever. The first marriage failed because the bride was unfaithful. This one cannot fail, because it rests on God's faithfulness, not hers.

The New Testament shows us the Bridegroom and the price. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her... so that he might present the church to himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph 5:25-27). The bride-price was his own life. Paul told the Corinthians, I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ (2 Cor 11:2). And the Bible ends with a wedding: the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready (Rev 19:7).

I will betroth you to me in faithfulness. And you shall know the LORD.

The goal of the marriage is this: you shall know the LORD. In the Bible, to know someone can mean the closest, most personal relationship. Israel had known about the LORD but had not truly known him. In the new covenant, God promises, they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest (Jer 31:34). And Jesus said, this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "And in that day I will answer, declares the LORD, I will answer the heavens, and they shall answer the earth, and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and they shall answer Jezreel, and I will sow her for myself in the land. And I will have mercy on No Mercy, and I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And in that day I will answer, declares the LORD, I will answer the heavens, and they shall answer the earth,

and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and they shall answer Jezreel,

Now the whole creation joins in a chain of answers. God answers the heavens, the heavens send rain to the earth, the earth answers with grain, wine and oil, and the crops answer Jezreel, God's people. The very things Israel once sought from Baal will flow freely from the true God. The one who gives rain is not Baal but the LORD.

and I will sow her for myself in the land. And I will have mercy on No Mercy, and I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God.'"

The ESV notes at verse 22 that Jezreel means "God will sow". Now God explains the name: I will sow her for myself in the land. The name that once meant scattering in judgment (1:4-5) now means planting in blessing.

And the three names of chapter 1 are all reversed. Jezreel is sown. No Mercy receives mercy. Not My People hears, You are my people. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew names are Lo-ruhama and Lo-ammi.) And the chapter ends with the simplest, most complete statement of what it means to belong to God. God says, You are my people, and the people answer, You are my God.

Paul quotes this verse to show that God's mercy reaches even the Gentiles: Those who were not my people I will call 'my people,' and her who was not beloved I will call 'beloved' (Rom 9:25). If you belong to Christ, this is your story. You were not his people. You had not received mercy. Now you have. And the covenant that joins you to him will last forever, because it rests on his faithfulness, not on yours.

2.title: I Will Betroth You to Me Forever
2.overview:
The children are to say to their brothers and sisters, "You are my people" and "You have received mercy" (v. 1).

The children are to plead with their mother, who is no longer a faithful wife, to put away her whoring, or she will be stripped naked, made like a wilderness and left to die of thirst. She has gone after her lovers, saying they give her bread, water, wool, flax, oil and drink. So God will hedge her way with thorns until she cannot find her lovers and decides to return to her first husband. She did not know that it was God who gave her grain, wine, oil, silver and gold, which were used for Baal (vv. 2-8).

Therefore God will take back his gifts, expose her before her lovers, end all her feasts, new moons and Sabbaths, lay waste her vines and fig trees, and punish her for the feast days of the Baals, when she adorned herself for her lovers and forgot him (vv. 9-13).

Therefore God will allure her into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her. He will give her vineyards back and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope, and she will answer as in the days of her youth, when she came out of Egypt. She will call God "My Husband", not "My Baal", and the names of the Baals will be removed. God will make a covenant with the creatures, abolish war and make her lie down in safety (vv. 14-18).

God will betroth her to himself forever in righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy and faithfulness, and she will know the LORD. In that day the heavens will answer the earth, the earth the grain, wine and oil, and they will answer Jezreel. God will sow her for himself in the land, have mercy on No Mercy and say to Not My People, "You are my people", and they will say, "You are my God" (vv. 19-23).
2.theology:
Idolatry is spiritual adultery that credits false gods with the gifts of the true God and seeks the gifts rather than the Giver (vv. 5, 8, 12; Deut 8:17-18; Rom 1:21; Jas 1:17).

God in mercy frustrates the paths of his wandering people and takes away his gifts to bring them back to himself (vv. 6-7, 9; Ps 119:67; Heb 12:6; Luke 15:17).

Religious activity mixed with idolatry is worthless before God, and forgetting God is the root of unfaithfulness (vv. 11, 13).

God's grace pursues the unfaithful, turning the place of trouble into a door of hope, fulfilled at the cross (vv. 14-15; Jer 2:2; Josh 7:25-26).

God removes idols from his people's hearts and brings peace to the whole creation (vv. 16-18; Jer 31:33; Isa 65:25; Rom 8:21).

God betroths his people to himself forever, supplying the righteousness, love and faithfulness the covenant requires, fulfilled in Christ the Bridegroom who gave himself for his church (vv. 19-20; Eph 5:25-27; 2 Cor 11:2; Rev 19:7; Jer 31:34; John 17:3).

God's mercy reverses the names of judgment and makes those who were not his people his own (vv. 1, 23; Rom 9:25; 1 Pet 2:10).
2.examples:
Children asked to plead with their own mother.

A woman who thinks her lovers pay for her bread.

A road blocked with thorns by a husband who wants his wife back.

Silver and gold from God melted into an idol.

A valley named Trouble turned into a door of hope.

A bridegroom who pays the whole bride-price himself.

"You are my people" answered by "You are my God."

3.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to me, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins."<sup>2</sup>So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.<sup>3</sup>And I said to her, "You must dwell as mine for many days. You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man; so will I also be to you."<sup>4</sup>For the children of Israel shall dwell many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or pillar, without ephod or household gods.<sup>5</sup>Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and they shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God says to Hosea, Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods (v. 1). Hosea buys her for fifteen shekels of silver and a measure and a half of barley (v. 2), and tells her she must live as his, faithful to him, so will I also be to you (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love pays the price to redeem an unfaithful people and restores them to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to me, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins."

Chapter 3 is only five verses long, but it is one of the clearest pictures of the gospel in the Old Testament prophets. Chapter 1 was told about Hosea. Now Hosea tells it himself: the LORD said to me.

The wife has left. She is now loved by another man and is an adulteress. Most readers understand this woman to be Gomer, since the word again and the whole story of the book point that way, though some think it was another woman. And God tells Hosea: Go again, love. Not "Go, forgive her if she comes back." Not "Go, bring her to justice." Go... love.

How could any man do that? Only by looking beyond himself to God: even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods. Hosea's love for Gomer was to be a copy of God's love for his people. God does not love his people because they are faithful. He loves them though they turn away.

The cakes of raisins were festive food. David once gave them to the people at a joyful celebration before the LORD (2 Sam 6:19). But here they are linked with the worship of other gods, probably eaten at pagan feasts. Israel loved the pleasures of false religion more than they loved God.

This is the love of God that the New Testament proclaims: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8). Not after we cleaned ourselves up. While we were still sinners. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us (1 John 4:10).

verseByVerse.quote: So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. And I said to her, "You must dwell as mine for many days. You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man; so will I also be to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley.

Hosea had to buy his own wife back. We are not told exactly why. Perhaps she had fallen into debt or slavery, or perhaps her lover demanded payment. Either way, she was not free, and someone had to pay.

The ESV notes that a shekel was about two-fifths of an ounce, a homer about six bushels and a lethech about three. So Hosea paid fifteen pieces of silver and about nine bushels of barley. Some have noticed that the law set the value of a slave at thirty shekels of silver (Exod 21:32), and suggest that Hosea paid half in silver and the rest in grain because he did not have enough money. If so, the price cost him everything he could scrape together. What is certain is that it was a real price, paid in full, for a wife who had betrayed him.

This is what redemption means. To redeem is to buy back by paying a price. And this is exactly what God did for us in Christ. You were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:18-19). Hosea paid silver and barley. Christ paid with his own life. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).

And I said to her, "You must dwell as mine for many days. You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man; so will I also be to you."

Redemption is not only rescue. It is belonging. You must dwell as mine. The price Hosea paid meant that she now belonged to him, and her old life must end: You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man. Paul says the same to Christians: You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body (1 Cor 6:19-20). Christ gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession (Titus 2:14).

But notice the last words: so will I also be to you. The commitment goes both ways. Hosea binds himself to her just as she is bound to him. Grace does not only demand faithfulness from us. It promises God's faithfulness to us.

There is also a period of waiting: many days. The relationship will be restored, but slowly, through a time of discipline in which the old ways are broken. The next verse explains what that means for Israel.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For the children of Israel shall dwell many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or pillar, without ephod or household gods (v. 4). Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and they shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Discipline prepares God's people to return to him and to the promised King from David's line.

verseByVerse.quote: For the children of Israel shall dwell many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or pillar, without ephod or household gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the children of Israel shall dwell many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or pillar, without ephod or household gods.

Just as Gomer would live many days set apart, Israel would go through a long season without the things it relied on. Without king or prince: no government of their own. Without sacrifice or pillar: no worship at the temple, but also no pagan sacred stones. Without ephod or household gods: the ephod was a priestly garment used in seeking God's guidance, and household gods were small idols people kept at home. God would take away both the true and the false supports together.

That is what exile did. The northern kingdom was destroyed by Assyria, and later Judah was carried to Babylon. God's people lost their kings and their temple. But in that long wilderness their hearts were being prepared to return.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and they shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and they shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days.

Afterward. Discipline is not the end. The children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God. Repentance is described as returning and seeking. They will come back to the husband they left.

And they will seek David their king. David had died more than two centuries before Hosea. So this cannot mean David himself. It means the promised King from David's family, the one the prophets looked for. Jeremiah spoke of David their king, whom I will raise up for them (Jer 30:9), and Ezekiel of one shepherd, my servant David (Ezek 34:23). This is the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Son of David. To return to God is to come to his King.

They shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness. The words fear and goodness belong together. Those who have been forgiven come trembling, knowing what they deserved, and amazed at the goodness they receive instead. In the latter days points to the time of fulfillment, the days that began with the coming of Christ.

So the story of Hosea's marriage is our story. We were the unfaithful bride. God did not abandon us. He came after us, paid the price to buy us back, and bound himself to us forever. The only right response is to return and seek the LORD our God, and his King, and come in reverent wonder to his goodness.

3.title: Go Again, Love
3.overview:
The LORD tells Hosea to go again and love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, just as the LORD loves Israel though they turn to other gods and love raisin cakes (v. 1).

Hosea buys her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. He tells her she must dwell as his for many days, not playing the whore or belonging to another man, and he will be the same toward her (vv. 2-3).

So Israel will live many days without king or prince, sacrifice or pillar, ephod or household gods. Afterward they will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king, and come in fear to the LORD and his goodness in the latter days (vv. 4-5).
3.theology:
God loves his people while they are unfaithful, and his love is the pattern for forgiving love (v. 1; Rom 5:8; 1 John 4:10).

Redemption is costly: the unfaithful are bought back at a price, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ (v. 2; 1 Pet 1:18-19; Mark 10:45).

Those who are redeemed belong to their Redeemer, and he binds himself to them in faithfulness (v. 3; 1 Cor 6:19-20; Titus 2:14).

God uses seasons of loss and discipline to strip away false supports and prepare his people to return (v. 4).

True repentance returns to the LORD and to the promised Son of David, and comes with reverent fear to his goodness (v. 5; Jer 30:9; Ezek 34:23-24).
3.examples:
A husband told to love his wife while she is with another man.

Fifteen pieces of silver and nine bushels of barley.

A wife who has to be bought back.

"You must dwell as mine... so will I also be to you."

A nation left without king, temple or idols.

Returning sinners trembling at God's goodness.

There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land;<sup>2</sup>there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break all bounds, and bloodshed follows bloodshed.<sup>3</sup>Therefore the land mourns, and all who dwell in it languish, and also the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens, and even the fish of the sea are taken away.<sup>4</sup>Yet let no one contend, and let none accuse, for with you is my contention, O priest.<sup>5</sup>You shall stumble by day; the prophet also shall stumble with you by night; and I will destroy your mother.<sup>6</sup>My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Brings a Case
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land (v. 1). Instead there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery (v. 2), and the land itself mourns (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: When a people loses the knowledge of God, every commandment falls, and even creation suffers.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land; there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break all bounds, and bloodshed follows bloodshed. Therefore the land mourns, and all who dwell in it languish, and also the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens, and even the fish of the sea are taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land;

Chapters 1-3 told Hosea's own story. From chapter 4 to the end, the book gathers his sermons to Israel. And the first one opens like a courtroom. The LORD has a controversy, a legal case, with the inhabitants of the land. God is both the one who brings the charge and the judge.

The charge begins with three things that are missing. No faithfulness: no one keeps their word. No steadfast love: no loyal, covenant love, toward God or toward one another. No knowledge of God: no real, personal acquaintance with the LORD and his ways. This third lack is the root of the other two. People who do not know God will not reflect his faithfulness and love.

there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break all bounds, and bloodshed follows bloodshed.

Listen to the list: lying, murder, stealing, adultery. It is almost a roll call of the Ten Commandments: You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness (Exod 20:13-16). When a nation forgets God, it does not become neutral. It breaks the commandments one by one until bloodshed follows bloodshed. In Hosea's day the northern kingdom saw one king after another murdered by the next.

Therefore the land mourns, and all who dwell in it languish, and also the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens, and even the fish of the sea are taken away.

Human sin wounds creation itself. The land dries up, and animals, birds and fish suffer. Paul says that the whole creation has been groaning together (Rom 8:22) because of the curse sin brought. What we do before God is never merely private.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's charge falls on the priests (vv. 4-5). My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me (v. 6). The priests feed on the sin of my people (vv. 7-8), and it shall be like people, like priest (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Leaders who fail to teach God's word lead God's people to ruin, and they will answer for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet let no one contend, and let none accuse, for with you is my contention, O priest. You shall stumble by day; the prophet also shall stumble with you by night; and I will destroy your mother. My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me. And since you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet let no one contend, and let none accuse, for with you is my contention, O priest.

Now God turns to the people most responsible: the priests. (The ESV notes that the verse could be read "your people are like those who contend with the priest"; either way, the priest is the one on trial.) The priests were supposed to teach Israel God's law. Instead they had let the nation slide into ignorance.

You shall stumble by day; the prophet also shall stumble with you by night; and I will destroy your mother.

Priest and false prophet will fall together, day and night. Your mother probably means the nation that the priest belonged to.

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me. And since you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your children.

This is one of the best-known verses in Hosea. My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. Notice the words my people. God still calls them his, and he grieves over them. They were not destroyed because the knowledge was unavailable. It was rejected. The priests had God's law and forgotten it.

The knowledge meant here is not just information. It is knowing God himself, his character and his word, in a way that shapes how we live. Malachi describes what a priest should be: the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth (Mal 2:7).

This is a solemn word for every pastor, teacher and parent. Those who are entrusted with God's truth will give an account for how they handed it on (Heb 13:17). And it is a word for every church. Biblical ignorance is not harmless. God's people are still destroyed for lack of knowledge.

verseByVerse.quote: The more they increased, the more they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame. They feed on the sin of my people; they are greedy for their iniquity. And it shall be like people, like priest; I will punish them for their ways and repay them for their deeds. They shall eat, but not be satisfied; they shall play the whore, but not multiply, because they have forsaken the LORD to cherish
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more they increased, the more they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame.

As the priesthood grew in number and wealth, it grew in sin. Success did not make them more faithful. It made them less.

They feed on the sin of my people; they are greedy for their iniquity.

This is a shocking charge. The ESV notes that sin can also be translated "sin offering". Under the law, priests received a share of the sin offerings to eat (Lev 6:26). So the more the people sinned, the more sin offerings they brought, and the more the priests ate. The priests had every reason to want the people to keep sinning. They were making a living from it. Instead of calling the people to repentance, they fed on their guilt.

Religion can still be turned into a business that profits from people's failures rather than healing them. God hates it.

And it shall be like people, like priest; I will punish them for their ways and repay them for their deeds.

Like people, like priest. The priests had sunk to the level of the people instead of lifting them up. And they would share the same judgment. Religious office gives no protection from God's justice.

They shall eat, but not be satisfied; they shall play the whore, but not multiply, because they have forsaken the LORD to cherish

They turned to Baal to get food and children, and they would get neither. Sin always promises satisfaction and never delivers it. The root cause is given plainly: they have forsaken the LORD. Jesus looked at crowds like this and saw them harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd (Matt 9:36).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Wine and whoredom take away the understanding (v. 11). The people consult pieces of wood and sacrifice on hilltops, and a spirit of whoredom has led them astray (vv. 12-13). God will not single out their daughters, for the men are worse (v. 14). Judah must not follow (v. 15). Israel is a stubborn heifer; Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone (vv. 16-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin darkens the mind and hardens the will, until God gives people over to what they have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: whoredom, wine, and new wine, which take away the understanding. My people inquire of a piece of wood, and their walking staff gives them oracles. For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray, and they have left their God to play the whore. They sacrifice on the tops of the mountains and burn offerings on the hills, under oak, poplar, and terebinth, because their shade is good. Therefore your daughters play the whore, and your brides commit adultery. I will not punish your daughters when they play the whore, nor your brides when they commit adultery; for the men themselves go aside with prostitutes and sacrifice with cult prostitutes, and a people without understanding shall come to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
whoredom, wine, and new wine, which take away the understanding.

Sexual sin and drunkenness take away the understanding. Sin is not only wrong. It makes people stupid. It clouds the mind until people cannot see what is obvious.

My people inquire of a piece of wood, and their walking staff gives them oracles. For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray, and they have left their God to play the whore.

Here is the result. God's people, who had the living God speaking through his prophets, were asking a piece of wood for guidance, probably a carved idol or sticks used for fortune-telling. The picture is almost comic, and deeply sad. That is what happens when the understanding is gone.

A spirit of whoredom had taken hold of them. Sin becomes a power, a spirit, that led them astray. They were no longer choosing freely. They were being driven.

They sacrifice on the tops of the mountains and burn offerings on the hills, under oak, poplar, and terebinth, because their shade is good. Therefore your daughters play the whore, and your brides commit adultery.

Pagan worship took place on hilltops and under shady trees, which were thought to be sacred. Notice the reason: because their shade is good. Their religion was chosen for comfort. And it included sexual rituals, which spread into the families. Fathers who worshipped this way saw their daughters and daughters-in-law follow them into immorality.

I will not punish your daughters when they play the whore, nor your brides when they commit adultery; for the men themselves go aside with prostitutes and sacrifice with cult prostitutes, and a people without understanding shall come to ruin.

This is a remarkable verse for its time. In that culture, women were usually blamed and punished for sexual sin while men often went free. God refuses that double standard. Why punish the young women when the men, their fathers and husbands, go aside with prostitutes in the name of religion? The fertility religion of Baal involved cult prostitutes at the shrines. God holds the men responsible for the corruption they led. God's justice does not favor the powerful.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you play the whore, O Israel, let not Judah become guilty. Enter not into Gilgal, nor go up to Beth-aven, and swear not, "As the LORD lives." Like a stubborn heifer, Israel is stubborn; can the LORD now feed them like a lamb in a broad pasture? Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone. When their drink is gone, they give themselves to whoring; their rulers dearly love shame. A wind has wrapped them in its wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though you play the whore, O Israel, let not Judah become guilty. Enter not into Gilgal, nor go up to Beth-aven, and swear not, "As the LORD lives."

Hosea warns the southern kingdom, Judah, not to follow Israel's example. Gilgal had once been a sacred place where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan, but it had become a center of corrupt worship. Beth-aven is most likely Hosea's scornful name for Bethel, where King Jeroboam I had set up a golden calf (1 Kgs 12:28-29; see 10:5). And swear not, "As the LORD lives": do not use God's name to bless worship that dishonors him. Mixing the LORD's name with idolatry was worse than silence.

Like a stubborn heifer, Israel is stubborn; can the LORD now feed them like a lamb in a broad pasture?

A stubborn young cow digs in its hooves and will not be led. How can God lead Israel like a lamb into a wide pasture when it refuses to move? God wanted to shepherd them into rest and plenty. Their stubbornness shut them out.

Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone.

Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, and the prophets often use its name for the whole nation. Here are some of the most frightening words in the book: leave him alone. There comes a point when God stops warning and lets people have what they have chosen. Paul describes the same judgment: God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts (Rom 1:24). The worst thing God can do to a sinner is to leave him alone with his sin.

When their drink is gone, they give themselves to whoring; their rulers dearly love shame.

A wind has wrapped them in its wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices.

Drinking leads to immorality, and the leaders (the ESV notes that the Hebrew calls them "shields", the ones who should have protected the people) love shame. But a wind is coming, the whirlwind of judgment, which will sweep them away. And their sacrifices, the religion they trusted, will only bring them shame.

Chapter 4 is dark, but it tells us what is at stake. The root of Israel's ruin was the loss of the knowledge of God. The cure is not better religious technique but knowing God himself, as he has made himself known in his word and, finally, in his Son. This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3).

4.title: No Knowledge of God in the Land
4.overview:
The LORD brings a case against Israel: there is no faithfulness, steadfast love or knowledge of God in the land, but swearing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery and bloodshed, so the land mourns and even the creatures waste away (vv. 1-3).

God's contention is with the priests. The people are destroyed for lack of knowledge because the priests rejected knowledge and forgot God's law, so God rejects them. The more they increased, the more they sinned; they feed on the people's sin. Priest and people will be punished alike; they will eat and not be satisfied, because they have forsaken the LORD (vv. 4-10).

Whoredom and wine take away understanding. The people consult wood and staffs, led astray by a spirit of whoredom, and sacrifice on hilltops under shady trees, while their daughters and brides fall into immorality. God will not punish the women, since the men themselves go to prostitutes and cult prostitutes. Judah is warned not to join Israel's worship at Gilgal and Beth-aven. Israel is a stubborn heifer; Ephraim is joined to idols and must be left alone, and a wind will sweep them away in shame (vv. 11-19).
4.theology:
The lack of faithfulness, steadfast love and knowledge of God leads to the breaking of all God's commandments and to the suffering of creation (vv. 1-3; Exod 20:13-16; Rom 8:22).

God's people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and those entrusted with teaching his word are especially accountable (vv. 4-6; Mal 2:7; Heb 13:17).

Religious leaders who profit from sin rather than calling people to repentance fall under God's judgment (vv. 7-9).

Sin never satisfies; it darkens the understanding and becomes an enslaving spirit (vv. 10-12).

God refuses a double standard and holds the powerful responsible for the corruption they lead (vv. 13-14).

Those who persist in idolatry may be given over by God to what they have chosen (v. 17; Rom 1:24).

The cure for a nation's ruin is the true knowledge of God, found in Jesus Christ (v. 6; John 17:3).
4.examples:
A courtroom where God is both accuser and judge.

A nation that breaks the commandments one by one.

Priests who grow fat on the people's sin offerings.

People asking a stick of wood for guidance.

Worship chosen because the shade is pleasant.

A stubborn heifer that will not be led to green pasture.

"Leave him alone."
