verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Snare and a Net
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Priests, people and king are summoned: the judgment is for you, for they have been a snare and a net (vv. 1-2). God knows Ephraim (v. 3). Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for the spirit of whoredom is within them (v. 4). They will seek the LORD with flocks and herds but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin binds people so that they cannot return, and ritual without repentance cannot find God.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O priests! Pay attention, O house of Israel! Give ear, O house of the king! For the judgment is for you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor. And the revolters have gone deep into slaughter, but I will discipline all of them. I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore; Israel is defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear this, O priests! Pay attention, O house of Israel! Give ear, O house of the king! For the judgment is for you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor.

Three groups are called to court: the priests, the house of Israel (the people) and the house of the king. Religious leaders, ordinary people and rulers are all guilty together.

They have been a snare and a net, like hunters' traps. Mizpah and Tabor were places on either side of the Jordan, perhaps sites of worship or royal authority. The places that should have drawn people to God had become traps that caught them in idolatry. Leaders who should protect God's people can become the very ones who lead them into sin.

And the revolters have gone deep into slaughter, but I will discipline all of them.

I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore; Israel is defiled.

I know Ephraim. Israel had lost the knowledge of God (4:1), but God had not lost his knowledge of Israel. Nothing was hidden. That truth is a terror for those who hide their sin, and a comfort for those who long to be fully known and still loved.

verseByVerse.quote: Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. For the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the LORD. The pride of Israel testifies to his face; Israel and Ephraim shall stumble in his guilt; Judah also shall stumble with them. With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them. They have dealt faithlessly with the LORD; for they have borne alien children. Now the new moon shall devour them with their fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. For the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the LORD.

This is one of the most sobering verses in the book. Their deeds do not permit them to return. Sin is not only something we do. It becomes something that holds us. The more they sinned, the less able they were to turn back. The spirit of whoredom is within them. Jesus said, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin (John 8:34). No one should imagine they can live in sin for years and then easily turn back whenever they choose. Only God's grace can break that grip.

The pride of Israel testifies to his face; Israel and Ephraim shall stumble in his guilt; Judah also shall stumble with them.

Israel's pride stands up in court as a witness against it. (The ESV notes that to his face may mean "in his presence".) And Judah, which was warned in 4:15, will fall too.

With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them.

Here is the tragedy of religion without repentance. They will bring animals to sacrifice. They will seek the LORD. But they will not find him. Why not? Because they wanted God's help without giving up their sin. Isaiah heard God say the same: What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? (Isa 1:11). God cannot be bought with offerings. He can only be found by those who turn to him with their whole heart.

They have dealt faithlessly with the LORD; for they have borne alien children. Now the new moon shall devour them with their fields.

Alien children may refer to children born of the fertility cult, or to a generation raised as strangers to God. Either way, the parents' unfaithfulness had produced children who did not belong to God. The new moon, a religious festival day, will not bring blessing but judgment on their harvests.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds in the towns of Benjamin (v. 8). Ephraim will become a desolation, and Judah's leaders, like landmark-movers, face God's wrath (vv. 9-11). God is like a moth and dry rot to them (v. 12). When they saw their sickness, they went to Assyria, But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound (v. 13). God will be like a lion and tear (v. 14): I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people must not seek healing from the powers of the world; God withdraws so that they will seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven; we follow you, O Benjamin! Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of punishment; among the tribes of Israel I make known what is sure. The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water. Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven; we follow you, O Benjamin!

Suddenly the scene becomes a war. Alarm horns sound in Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven, towns in the territory of Benjamin, on the border between Israel and Judah. (The ESV notes that the last phrase may be "after you", a battle cry.)

Many think this describes the war of about 734-732 BC, when Israel joined with Syria to attack Judah, and Judah's King Ahaz called on Assyria for help (2 Kgs 16:5-9; Isa 7:1-2). The two halves of God's people were fighting each other, and both were about to be crushed by a foreign empire.

Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of punishment; among the tribes of Israel I make known what is sure.

The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water.

Moving a boundary stone was a way of stealing a neighbor's land, and God's law forbade it (Deut 19:14). The leaders of Judah were doing on a national scale what thieves did on a small one, grabbing territory in the chaos of war.

Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth.

Ephraim was determined to go its own way. (The ESV notes that filth may mean "to follow human precepts".) Its suffering was the result of a settled choice.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like dry rot to the house of Judah. When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to the great king. But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound. For I will be like a lion to Ephraim, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear and go away; I will carry off, and no one shall rescue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like dry rot to the house of Judah.

God describes his judgment with two quiet, frightening pictures. A moth eats through clothing unseen. Dry rot eats through wood from the inside. Nothing seems to happen, and then one day the garment falls apart or the beam gives way. God's judgment is not always sudden. Sometimes it is a slow decay that goes unnoticed until it is too late.

When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to the great king. But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound.

Both kingdoms finally noticed they were sick. But instead of turning to God, they went to Assyria, the superpower of the day. King Menahem of Israel paid Assyria a fortune in silver for support (2 Kgs 15:19-20), and King Ahaz of Judah begged, I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me (2 Kgs 16:7). (The ESV notes that the great king may be a name, "King Jareb".)

But he is not able to cure you. The world's powers cannot heal what is wrong with God's people. The same Assyria they ran to would destroy Israel. Every generation of believers is tempted to look for rescue in politics, money or human strength instead of in God. In returning and rest you shall be saved, God said through Isaiah, But you were unwilling (Isa 30:15).

For I will be like a lion to Ephraim, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear and go away; I will carry off, and no one shall rescue.

The moth becomes a lion. The slow decay turns into a sudden attack. And notice who the lion is. Not Assyria, but God: I, even I, will tear. Assyria would only be the instrument. Behind every judgment of history stands the Lord of history.

verseByVerse.quote: I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.

After tearing, the lion goes back to its den and waits. God withdraws. But the verse contains one word full of hope: until. God's absence has a purpose. He waits until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face.

Notice what God is waiting for. Not better sacrifices, not political alliances, but two things: confessing their guilt and seeking his face. In their distress earnestly seek me. God sometimes lets his people come to the end of themselves so that they will finally look for him.

That is exactly what the prodigal son did. When he came to himself, he said, I will arise and go to my father, and while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him (Luke 15:17-20). The God who withdraws is watching the road. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (Jas 4:8). The next chapter begins with the words he is waiting to hear, Come, let us return to the LORD, though chapter 6 will ask whether the people mean them.

5.title: Until They Seek My Face
5.overview:
Priests, the people of Israel and the royal house are called to judgment, for they have been a snare at Mizpah and a net on Tabor. God knows Ephraim and its defilement (vv. 1-3).

Their deeds keep them from returning to God, for a spirit of whoredom is within them and they do not know the LORD. Israel's pride testifies against it, and Israel, Ephraim and Judah will stumble. They will seek the LORD with their flocks and herds but will not find him, for he has withdrawn; they have been faithless and borne alien children (vv. 4-7).

The alarm is sounded at Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven. Ephraim will become a desolation; Judah's princes are like those who move landmarks, and God will pour out his wrath on them (vv. 8-11).

God is like a moth to Ephraim and dry rot to Judah. When they saw their sickness, they went to Assyria, but the great king could not heal them. God will be like a lion, tearing and carrying off with no one to rescue. Then he will return to his place until they acknowledge their guilt and earnestly seek his face (vv. 12-15).
5.theology:
Religious leaders, people and rulers are all accountable to God, and nothing is hidden from him (vv. 1-3).

Persistent sin enslaves, so that people cannot return to God without his grace (v. 4; John 8:34).

Religious ritual without repentance cannot find God (v. 6; Isa 1:11).

God's judgment may work slowly like decay or suddenly like a lion, and he stands behind the powers he uses (vv. 12, 14).

God's people must not seek from the world's powers the healing only God can give (v. 13; Isa 30:15).

God withdraws in order to bring his people to confess their guilt and seek his face, and he receives those who return (v. 15; Luke 15:17-20; Jas 4:8).
5.examples:
Places of worship turned into hunters' traps.

A people who could not return because their sins held them.

Worshippers who bring their flocks and cannot find God.

A moth in the closet and rot in the beams.

A sick nation asking the superpower for a cure.

A lion that tears and then waits in its den.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up (v. 1). After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him (v. 2). Let us press on to know the LORD; he will come like the dawn and the spring rains (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him, and raises them up to live before him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up.

At the end of chapter 5 God said he would withdraw until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face (5:15). Now we hear words of return: Come, let us return to the LORD.

These words are beautiful, and they are exactly right. The God who tears is the God who heals. The lion of 5:14 is also the physician. He has torn us, that he may heal us. God's wounds are never meant to destroy his people but to bring them back. The same hand that strikes is the hand that binds up.

But who is speaking, and do they mean it? Christians have read these verses in two ways. Many believe they are the words of the people, a quick, easy repentance that assumes God will simply fix everything, and that God's sad reply in verse 4 shows it was not real. Others believe this is Hosea himself calling the people to genuine repentance, a pattern of what true return looks like. Both readings teach something important. The words are true. The question is whether they come from the heart. It is possible to say all the right things about returning to God and still not return.

verseByVerse.quote: After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him. Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD; his going out is sure as the dawn; he will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him.

After two days... on the third day is a way of saying "very soon". Those speaking are confident that God's healing will come quickly, and that he will revive the nation, raising it up from its sickness as if from death, that we may live before him.

Many Christians have heard in this verse a pointer to something greater. Jesus said, Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead (Luke 24:46), and Paul says Christ was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Cor 15:4). Neither passage names Hosea, and we should not claim more than the text says. But the pattern is striking. Israel hoped to be raised up on the third day to live before God. That hope was finally fulfilled in the one true Israelite, Jesus, who was raised on the third day, and in whom all who belong to him are raised to new life. Our hope of revival is not in our own quick repentance but in his resurrection.

Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD; his going out is sure as the dawn; he will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth."

The missing knowledge of God (4:1, 6) is exactly what they now long for: let us press on to know the LORD. And they are sure God will come, as sure as the sunrise, as refreshing as the spring rains that make the crops grow. Notice the contrast with Baal. They had worshipped Baal to get rain. The true rain comes from the LORD.

For Christians, this is a good prayer to make our own: let us press on to know the LORD. Knowing God is not a single moment but a lifelong pursuit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Your Love Is Like a Morning Cloud
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? Their love vanishes like the dew that goes early away (v. 4), so God has struck them through the prophets (v. 5). For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (v. 6). But like Adam they transgressed the covenant (v. 7); Gilead and the priests are stained with blood (vv. 8-10), and a harvest of judgment is appointed for Judah too (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: God is not satisfied with religious ritual; he desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away. Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth as the light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away.

Now God answers, and his answer sounds like a heartbroken parent: What shall I do with you? God is not puzzled. He is grieved.

The problem is not that they never loved God. It is that their love does not last. It is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away. In the Middle East, a morning mist can promise rain, and dew covers everything at dawn. But when the sun rises, both are gone within an hour. Israel's repentance was like that: real feeling, gone by midmorning.

Many of us know this kind of love for God. A moving sermon, a crisis, a season of revival, and we are full of devotion. A week later it has evaporated. God does not want morning-dew religion. He wants steadfast love, love that lasts through the heat of the day. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation, Paul says, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor 7:10). The difference is whether it changes the heart.

Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth as the light.

Because their love was so shallow, God sent the prophets with words that cut like an axe. God's word is not only comfort. It wounds in order to heal. And God's judgment goes forth as the light. It is clear, open and impossible to escape.

verseByVerse.quote: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

This is perhaps the best-known verse in Hosea, and one of the most important in the Old Testament.

God does not reject sacrifice altogether. He commanded it. But he says that what he truly wants is steadfast love, loyal covenant love toward him and toward others, and the knowledge of God. Sacrifices without love and knowledge are worthless to him. Samuel said it long before: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22). Micah, preaching in the same years, said it too: what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (Mic 6:8). David understood it: The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Ps 51:17).

Jesus quoted this verse twice. When the Pharisees criticized him for eating with tax collectors and sinners, he said, Go and learn what this means: 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.' For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Matt 9:13). And when they condemned his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, he said, if you had known what this means, 'I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,' you would not have condemned the guiltless (Matt 12:7). (Jesus' wording follows the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which, as the ESV notes, reads "mercy".)

Religious people are always tempted to think that God is pleased with correct ritual, church attendance and religious duties, while their hearts remain cold and their treatment of others is hard. God says no. What he desires is love for him and mercy toward people. And Christ himself fulfilled this verse perfectly. He offered the one sacrifice that truly pleased God, and he offered it out of steadfast love.

verseByVerse.quote: But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me. Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood. As robbers lie in wait for a man, so the priests band together; they murder on the way to Shechem; they commit villainy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me.

This verse is debated. Some understand like Adam to refer to the first man. Just as Adam broke the command God gave him in Eden, Israel broke its covenant. Many Reformed theologians have pointed to this verse as evidence that God's relationship with Adam in the garden was a covenant. Others note the word there and think it refers to a place, the town called Adam by the Jordan, where Israel crossed into the land (Josh 3:16), perhaps the site of some act of unfaithfulness we no longer know. Both readings are possible.

Either way, the charge is clear: they transgressed the covenant. And if the first reading is right, it reminds us of something the whole Bible teaches. All humanity sinned in Adam. Israel's failure was the same failure repeated. That is why we need another Adam who would keep covenant perfectly, the one Paul calls the one who was to come (Rom 5:14), Jesus Christ.

Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood.

As robbers lie in wait for a man, so the priests band together; they murder on the way to Shechem; they commit villainy.

The examples are shocking. A town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, has blood on its streets. And the priests behave like a gang of highway robbers, ambushing travelers on the road to Shechem. Shechem was one of the cities of refuge, where people could flee for protection. The priests turned the road to safety into a place of murder. The people who should have been shepherds had become wolves.

verseByVerse.quote: In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; Ephraim's whoredom is there; Israel is defiled. For you also, O Judah, a harvest is appointed. When I restore the fortunes of my people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; Ephraim's whoredom is there; Israel is defiled.

God has seen it himself: a horrible thing. The unfaithfulness of his people is not a small matter to him. It horrifies him.

For you also, O Judah, a harvest is appointed. When I restore the fortunes of my people,

Judah too will reap what it has sown: a harvest is appointed. The last line, When I restore the fortunes of my people, begins a sentence that continues into chapter 7. Even in a chapter of judgment, God speaks of restoring his people. He has not given up. But first he must deal with their sin.

Chapter 6 holds together two truths we need. God truly heals those who return to him, and he raises them up to live before him. But he is not fooled by morning-dew religion. He desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself. The only one who has ever offered God both perfectly is Jesus Christ, and it is in him, crucified and raised on the third day, that we can return and live.

6.title: Steadfast Love and Not Sacrifice
6.overview:
"Come, let us return to the LORD," the call goes; he has torn and struck, and he will heal and bind up. After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up to live before him. Let us press on to know the LORD, whose coming is as sure as the dawn and the spring rains (vv. 1-3).

God asks what he should do with Ephraim and Judah, whose love is like a morning cloud and early dew. So he has hewn them by the prophets and slain them by his words. He desires steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings (vv. 4-6).

Like Adam they transgressed the covenant and dealt faithlessly. Gilead is tracked with blood, and priests murder like robbers on the road to Shechem. God has seen a horrible thing in Israel. A harvest is appointed for Judah also, when God restores the fortunes of his people (vv. 7-11).
6.theology:
The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him (v. 1).

God revives his people and raises them up to live before him, a hope fulfilled in Christ, raised on the third day (v. 2; Luke 24:46; 1 Cor 15:4).

Knowing God is a lifelong pursuit (v. 3).

Shallow, passing devotion does not satisfy God; true repentance changes the heart (v. 4; 2 Cor 7:10).

God desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself more than religious ritual, as Jesus taught (v. 6; Matt 9:13; 12:7; 1 Sam 15:22; Mic 6:8; Ps 51:17).

Israel repeated Adam's covenant-breaking, and all humanity needs the last Adam, Jesus Christ (v. 7; Rom 5:14).
6.examples:
A lion that tears in order to heal.

A promise of rising on the third day.

Love that vanishes like morning mist.

A worshipper with perfect attendance and a cold heart.

Jesus eating with sinners and quoting Hosea.

Priests ambushing travelers on the road to a city of refuge.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When God would heal Israel, its evil is exposed: lies, theft and raids (v. 1). They forget that God remembers all their evil (v. 2). The leaders delight in treachery, and They are all adulterers, burning like an oven (vv. 3-4). Plotting smolders all night and blazes in the morning; they devour their rulers. All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Hearts inflamed by lust for power consume leaders and nations, while no one calls on God.

verseByVerse.quote: when I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed, and the evil deeds of Samaria, for they deal falsely; the thief breaks in, and the bandits raid outside. But they do not consider that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds surround them; they are before my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
when I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed, and the evil deeds of Samaria, for they deal falsely; the thief breaks in, and the bandits raid outside.

This verse completes the sentence that began at the end of chapter 6: When I restore the fortunes of my people, when I would heal Israel... Every time God comes near to heal, he finds fresh sin. Like a doctor who pulls back the bandage to treat a wound and finds infection everywhere, God's desire to heal exposes how sick Israel is. Inside the houses, thieves break in. Outside, bandits raid. Society is coming apart.

But they do not consider that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds surround them; they are before my face.

Their great mistake was to think God forgets. They do not consider that I remember. Sin that people have long forgotten is still before my face. Their own deeds now surround them like witnesses crowding around in court. The only way for sin to be forgotten by God is for it to be forgiven.

verseByVerse.quote: By their evil they make the king glad, and the princes by their treachery. They are all adulterers; they are like a heated oven whose baker ceases to stir the fire, from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened. On the day of our king, the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers. For with hearts like an oven they approach their intrigue; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire. All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By their evil they make the king glad, and the princes by their treachery.

The rulers enjoy the wickedness around them. They are amused by it, and they reward it. When leaders delight in evil, a nation is in deep trouble.

They are all adulterers; they are like a heated oven whose baker ceases to stir the fire, from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened.

Now comes an extended picture. A baker lights his oven at night and lets the fire smolder while the dough rises. In the morning he stirs it and it blazes. The people are like that: their passions, both sexual and political, smolder quietly and then burst into flame.

On the day of our king, the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers.

For with hearts like an oven they approach their intrigue; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire.

The scene seems to be a royal celebration. The king and his officials drink themselves sick, and the king joins hands with mockers. Meanwhile, conspirators wait for their moment. All night they plot. In the morning they strike.

All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me.

This describes exactly what happened in Hosea's lifetime. Of the last six kings of Israel, four were murdered by the men who replaced them. Shallum killed Zechariah, Menahem killed Shallum, Pekah killed Pekahiah, and Hoshea killed Pekah (2 Kgs 15:10, 14, 25, 30). The throne was passed from one assassin to the next.

And the saddest line is the last: none of them calls upon me. In all the turmoil, not one king or plotter turned to God. A nation in crisis ran through leaders like fuel and never once prayed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim mixes himself with the peoples; Ephraim is a cake not turned (v. 8). Strangers drain his strength, and gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not (v. 9). Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense, calling to Egypt, going to Assyria (v. 11), so God will catch them in his net (v. 12). I would redeem them, but they speak lies against me (v. 13). They wail but not to God from the heart (v. 14); They return, but not upward (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Compromise with the world leaves God's people half-baked, blind to their decline and turning everywhere except to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim mixes himself with the peoples; Ephraim is a cake not turned. Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not. The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him, for all this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim mixes himself with the peoples; Ephraim is a cake not turned.

Israel mixes himself with the peoples, blending its faith and life with the nations around it, their gods, their politics and their ways. The result is a cake not turned. Picture a flat bread cooked on hot stones and never flipped: burned black on one side, raw dough on the other. Useless.

That is what happens when God's people try to belong half to God and half to the world. They end up neither truly godly nor truly worldly, just half-baked. The world does not respect them, and God cannot use them.

Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not.

Twice we read, he knows it not. Foreign powers were draining Israel's wealth through heavy tribute, and Israel did not notice. Gray hairs, signs of age and decline, had appeared, and no one saw them. The nation thought it was still young and strong.

This is one of the most dangerous conditions a person or church can be in. Spiritual decline rarely announces itself. It creeps in, like gray hairs, until one day the strength is gone. Samson woke up and said he would go out as before, But he did not know that the LORD had left him (Judg 16:20). Exhort one another every day... that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin (Heb 3:13).

The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him, for all this.

For all this: all the disasters, the murdered kings, the tribute, the decline. Yet they do not return. Suffering alone does not bring people back to God. Pride keeps them from it. (The ESV notes that to his face may mean "in his presence".)

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense, calling to Egypt, going to Assyria. As they go, I will spread over them my net; I will bring them down like birds of the heavens; I will discipline them according to the report made to their congregation. Woe to them, for they have strayed from me! Destruction to them, for they have rebelled against me! I would redeem them, but they speak lies against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense, calling to Egypt, going to Assyria.

Now another picture: a silly dove, fluttering first one way and then the other. Israel's foreign policy was just like that. One king paid tribute to Assyria, and then the last king, Hoshea, secretly asked So, king of Egypt for help against Assyria (2 Kgs 17:3-4). They flew back and forth between the superpowers, looking for safety everywhere except in God. It was without sense, because neither Egypt nor Assyria could save them.

As they go, I will spread over them my net; I will bring them down like birds of the heavens; I will discipline them according to the report made to their congregation.

A bird that flies about carelessly ends up in the hunter's net. God himself is the hunter. Their scheming would lead straight into his judgment, just as they had been warned.

Woe to them, for they have strayed from me! Destruction to them, for they have rebelled against me! I would redeem them, but they speak lies against me.

Here is God's heart in the middle of judgment: I would redeem them. God wanted to save them. What stood in the way was not his unwillingness but their lies. Jesus wept over Jerusalem with the same sorrow: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! (Matt 23:37).

verseByVerse.quote: They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds; for grain and wine they gash themselves; they rebel against me. Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me. They return, but not upward; they are like a treacherous bow; their princes shall fall by the sword because of the insolence of their tongue. This shall be their derision in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds; for grain and wine they gash themselves; they rebel against me.

They did cry out, but not to me from the heart. They wailed on their beds about their troubles. And to get grain and wine, they gash themselves, cutting their bodies as the prophets of Baal did on Mount Carmel, who cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances (1 Kgs 18:28). They were desperate enough to bleed for a harvest, but not humble enough to turn to the God who gives the harvest.

There is a difference between being sorry for our troubles and being sorry for our sin. Many people cry out when life hurts. Not everyone cries out to God from the heart.

Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me.

God had given Israel its strength, trained it like a father teaching a son to fight. And they used that strength to plot against him. Every gift we turn against God is doubly ungrateful.

They return, but not upward; they are like a treacherous bow; their princes shall fall by the sword because of the insolence of their tongue. This shall be their derision in the land of Egypt.

They return, but not upward. (The ESV notes it may mean "not to the Most High".) They turned, but in the wrong direction. They turned to Egypt, to Assyria, to Baal, but never up to God. They are like a treacherous bow, a warped bow whose arrows never hit the target. And the Egypt they trusted would one day laugh at them.

True repentance is not just turning away from trouble. It is turning upward, to God. And the good news of the gospel is that when we turn upward, we find that God has already come down to us in Christ.

7.title: A Cake Not Turned
7.overview:
Whenever God would heal Israel, Ephraim's iniquity is exposed: falsehood, theft and raids. They forget that God remembers their evil, and their deeds surround them before his face. The king and princes delight in treachery. All are adulterers, burning like an oven whose fire smolders overnight; at a royal feast the princes are sick with wine, while conspirators plot all night and blaze in the morning. They devour their rulers; all their kings have fallen, and none calls on God (vv. 1-7).

Ephraim mixes with the nations and is a cake not turned. Foreigners devour his strength and gray hairs appear, and he does not know it. Though pride testifies against him, he does not return to God. Ephraim is like a silly dove calling to Egypt and going to Assyria, so God will spread his net over them. Woe to them for straying; God would redeem them, but they lie against him. They wail on their beds and gash themselves for grain and wine, but do not cry to God from the heart. Though God strengthened them, they plot evil; they return, but not upward, like a treacherous bow, and their princes will fall and be mocked in Egypt (vv. 8-16).
7.theology:
God remembers all sin until it is forgiven, and his desire to heal exposes the depth of sin (vv. 1-2).

Lust for power and pleasure consumes leaders and nations, especially when no one calls on God (vv. 3-7).

Mixing with the world leaves God's people half-baked, and spiritual decline often goes unnoticed (vv. 8-9; Judg 16:20; Heb 3:13).

Trusting in worldly powers instead of God is senseless and ends in judgment (vv. 11-12; 2 Kgs 17:3-4).

God longs to redeem, but sinners refuse him (v. 13; Matt 23:37).

Crying out over troubles is not the same as crying to God from the heart; true repentance turns upward to God (vv. 14-16).
7.examples:
A doctor who lifts the bandage and finds infection everywhere.

A throne passed from one assassin to the next.

A flatbread burned on one side and raw on the other.

Gray hairs nobody notices.

A dove fluttering between two superpowers.

People who bleed for a harvest but will not pray.

A warped bow that never hits the target.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Made Kings, but Not Through Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The alarm sounds, for the enemy swoops like a vulture because Israel has broken God's covenant (v. 1). They cry, My God, we—Israel—know you, but they have spurned the good (vv. 2-3). They made kings, but not through me, and made idols of silver and gold (v. 4). God spurns the calf of Samaria: a craftsman made it; it is not God (vv. 5-6). For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Religious words cannot cover a life that rejects God's rule, and those who sow emptiness will reap destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Set the trumpet to your lips! One like a vulture is over the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law. To me they cry, "My God, we—Israel—know you." Israel has spurned the good; the enemy shall pursue him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set the trumpet to your lips! One like a vulture is over the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law.

Blow the alarm! An enemy is circling like a vulture (or an eagle) over God's people, ready to swoop. The enemy was Assyria. The house of the LORD here most likely means God's land and people, his household. And the reason is plain: they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law. The danger from outside was the result of sin inside.

To me they cry, "My God, we—Israel—know you."

What a claim. My God, we—Israel—know you. They insist they know God. They say the right words. But chapter 4 has already told us there was no knowledge of God in the land (4:1). Their confession was empty.

Jesus warned about the same thing: Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father. Many will say they did great things in his name, And then will I declare to them, 'I never knew you' (Matt 7:21-23). The question is not whether we claim to know God, but whether he knows us as his own.

Israel has spurned the good; the enemy shall pursue him.

They rejected the good, God himself and his ways, so they would be pursued by the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: They made kings, but not through me. They set up princes, but I knew it not. With their silver and gold they made idols for their own destruction. I have spurned your calf, O Samaria. My anger burns against them. How long will they be incapable of innocence? For it is from Israel; a craftsman made it; it is not God. The calf of Samaria shall be broken to pieces. For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. The standing grain has no heads; it shall yield no flour; if it were to yield, strangers would devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They made kings, but not through me. They set up princes, but I knew it not. With their silver and gold they made idols for their own destruction.

Two sins stand side by side. First, They made kings, but not through me. The northern kingdom's kings came to power by murder and conspiracy (7:7), not by God's choosing. They ran their politics without asking God. Second, they made idols out of the silver and gold God had given them (2:8). Both were ways of taking control away from God, in government and in worship.

I have spurned your calf, O Samaria. My anger burns against them. How long will they be incapable of innocence?

Your calf, O Samaria refers to the golden calves that King Jeroboam I had set up at Bethel and Dan two centuries earlier, telling the people, Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt (1 Kgs 12:28). The people probably thought of the calf as a pedestal for the LORD or a symbol of his power. God calls it an idol and rejects it. (The ESV notes that I have spurned is literally "He has spurned".)

How long will they be incapable of innocence? God asks the question with sorrow. They had become so used to sin that they could no longer imagine living without it.

For it is from Israel; a craftsman made it; it is not God. The calf of Samaria shall be broken to pieces.

Here is the simple truth about every idol: a craftsman made it; it is not God. Something people made cannot save the people who made it. Isaiah mocked the man who uses half a log to cook his dinner and makes the other half into a god and prays to it and says, "Deliver me, for you are my god!" (Isa 44:17). The calf would be smashed. (The ESV notes the phrase may mean it "shall go up in flames".)

For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. The standing grain has no heads; it shall yield no flour; if it were to yield, strangers would devour it.

This is one of the most memorable sayings in the Bible. They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. What they planted was empty, nothing but wind: idols, political schemes, false confidence. But what they would harvest was a tornado of destruction. Sin always yields more than it sows. Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

And the harvest they did grow would fail: stalks with no grain, and if any grain came, foreign armies would eat it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Israel Has Forgotten His Maker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is swallowed up among the nations, a useless vessel, having hired lovers in Assyria (vv. 8-10). Their many altars have become altars for sinning, and God's law is treated as a strange thing (vv. 11-12). God does not accept their sacrifices; they shall return to Egypt (v. 13). For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities, but fire will devour them (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who forget their Maker and trust in their own security will lose everything they built.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel is swallowed up; already they are among the nations as a useless vessel. For they have gone up to Assyria, a wild donkey wandering alone; Ephraim has hired lovers. Though they hire allies among the nations, I will soon gather them up. And the king and princes shall soon writhe because of the tribute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is swallowed up; already they are among the nations as a useless vessel.

Israel wanted to be like the nations. Now it was being swallowed by them. It had become a useless vessel, like a cracked pot no one wants. God's people were meant to be a treasured possession. By imitating the world, they became worthless to it.

For they have gone up to Assyria, a wild donkey wandering alone; Ephraim has hired lovers.

A wild donkey is stubborn and independent. Even donkeys in the wild keep to their herd, but this one wanders alone. Israel had left God and gone off on its own to Assyria. And Ephraim has hired lovers. The picture is shocking. A prostitute is normally paid, but Israel was paying its lovers. That was the tribute Israel's kings paid to Assyria to buy protection (2 Kgs 15:19-20; 17:3).

Though they hire allies among the nations, I will soon gather them up. And the king and princes shall soon writhe because of the tribute.

The protection money would crush them. The kings of Israel would writhe under the burden of paying it. Alliances bought with money are chains, not safety.

verseByVerse.quote: Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they have become to him altars for sinning. Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing. As for my sacrificial offerings, they sacrifice meat and eat it, but the LORD does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins; they shall return to Egypt. For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities; so I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour her strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they have become to him altars for sinning.

Israel built many altars, supposedly to deal with sin. But because they were used for false worship, the altars themselves became places of more sin. Religion without truth does not remove sin. It multiplies it.

Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing.

The problem was not that Israel lacked God's law. God could write it down ten thousand times, and they would still treat it as a strange thing, something foreign that had nothing to do with them. It is possible to have Bibles in every room and still treat God's word as strange.

As for my sacrificial offerings, they sacrifice meat and eat it, but the LORD does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins; they shall return to Egypt.

Their sacrifices had become nothing more than barbecues. They killed animals, ate the meat and enjoyed the feast, but God did not accept any of it. And the punishment would be a terrible reversal: they shall return to Egypt. God had brought them out of slavery in Egypt. Now they would go back into bondage. Moses had warned that disobedience would bring them back in ships to Egypt, a journey that I promised that you should never make again (Deut 28:68). Egypt here stands for slavery and exile, which Assyria would soon bring.

For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities; so I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour her strongholds.

Here is the root: Israel has forgotten his Maker. And what does forgetfulness of God look like? Building palaces and fortified cities. They trusted in wealth and walls. Judah did it too. And God would send fire on both. Assyria destroyed Samaria's palaces, and later Sennacherib came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them (2 Kgs 18:13).

People still forget their Maker in the same way: not usually by openly rejecting him, but by building their own security and forgetting they need him. The only security that cannot be burned is the kingdom Christ gives, a kingdom that cannot be shaken (Heb 12:28).

8.title: They Sow the Wind
8.overview:
The trumpet is to sound, for an enemy like a vulture is over the LORD's house because Israel has broken his covenant and rebelled against his law. They cry that they know God, but they have spurned the good, and the enemy will pursue them. They made kings and princes without God and idols from their silver and gold. God spurns the calf of Samaria: a craftsman made it; it is not God, and it will be broken. They sow the wind and will reap the whirlwind; their grain will fail or be devoured by strangers (vv. 1-7).

Israel is swallowed up among the nations as a useless vessel. Like a wild donkey alone they went to Assyria and hired lovers; the king and princes will writhe under the tribute. Ephraim's many altars have become altars for sinning, and God's law is treated as strange. God does not accept their sacrifices; he will punish their sins, and they will return to Egypt. Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, Judah has multiplied fortified cities, and God will send fire on their strongholds (vv. 8-14).
8.theology:
Claiming to know God is worthless without the life that shows it (vv. 2-3; Matt 7:21-23).

Governing without God and worshipping idols of human making are two forms of the same rebellion (vv. 4-6; 1 Kgs 12:28; Isa 44:17).

Those who sow emptiness reap destruction far greater than what they sowed (v. 7; Gal 6:7-8).

God's people who imitate the world become useless to it, and alliances bought with money become chains (vv. 8-10).

False worship multiplies sin, and having God's word is no benefit to those who treat it as strange (vv. 11-13).

Forgetting the Maker and trusting in human security brings judgment on everything built without him (vv. 13-14; Deut 28:68; 2 Kgs 18:13).
8.examples:
A people who say, "We know you," and do not.

Kings crowned by conspiracy without a prayer.

A golden calf made by a craftsman and called a god.

Wind sown, and a whirlwind harvested.

A nation paying its lovers.

A Bible in every room treated as a strange book.

Palaces and walls built by people who forgot their Maker.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Days of Punishment Have Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rejoice not, O Israel! They have loved a prostitute's wages on the threshing floors, so the harvest will fail (vv. 1-2). They will not remain in the LORD's land but go to Egypt and Assyria, where their offerings will be unclean (vv. 3-4). What will they do on the festival day when they are gone into exile (vv. 5-6)? The days of punishment have come; the people call the prophet a fool, though he is the watchman, for they have corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Festivals without faithfulness end in exile, and those who mock God's watchmen cannot escape his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice not, O Israel! Exult not like the peoples; for you have played the whore, forsaking your God. You have loved a prostitute's wages on all threshing floors. Threshing floor and wine vat shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail them. They shall not remain in the land of the LORD, but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean food in Assyria. They shall not pour drink offerings of wine to the LORD, and their sacrifices shall not please him. It shall be like mourners' bread to them; all who eat of it shall be defiled; for their bread shall be for their hunger only; it shall not come to the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice not, O Israel! Exult not like the peoples; for you have played the whore, forsaking your God. You have loved a prostitute's wages on all threshing floors.

The setting may be a harvest festival. The grain has been gathered on the threshing floors, the flat open spaces where it was separated from the chaff, and the people are celebrating. Hosea interrupts the party: Rejoice not. They were thanking Baal for the harvest, as though it were the wages he had paid them for their devotion. God calls it a prostitute's wages.

Threshing floor and wine vat shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail them.

The harvest they credited to Baal would fail. God would take back his gifts (2:9).

They shall not remain in the land of the LORD, but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean food in Assyria.

Notice what the land is called: the land of the LORD. It was never really Israel's. It was God's land, given to them to live in as his people. If they would not live as his people, they could not stay in his land. Some would flee to Egypt. Others would be carried to Assyria, where they could not keep God's food laws. Ezekiel later described the same judgment: Thus shall the people of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations (Ezek 4:13).

They shall not pour drink offerings of wine to the LORD, and their sacrifices shall not please him. It shall be like mourners' bread to them; all who eat of it shall be defiled; for their bread shall be for their hunger only; it shall not come to the house of the LORD.

In exile, there would be no temple and no offerings. Their food would be like mourners' bread, eaten in a house where someone had died, which made everyone who ate it ceremonially unclean (Num 19:14). All their meals would be merely for survival, for their hunger only. Nothing could be offered to God. Life without worship is just eating to stay alive.

verseByVerse.quote: What will you do on the day of the appointed festival, and on the day of the feast of the LORD? For behold, they are going away from destruction; but Egypt shall gather them; Memphis shall bury them. Nettles shall possess their precious things of silver; thorns shall be in their tents. The days of punishment have come; the days of recompense have come; Israel shall know it. The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad, because of your great iniquity and great hatred. The prophet is the watchman of Ephraim with my God; yet a fowler's snare is on all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God. They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah: he will remember their iniquity; he will punish their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What will you do on the day of the appointed festival, and on the day of the feast of the LORD?

A painful question. When the great feast days come around in exile, what will they do? No temple, no sacrifices, no celebration. They had corrupted the feasts. Now they would lose them.

For behold, they are going away from destruction; but Egypt shall gather them; Memphis shall bury them. Nettles shall possess their precious things of silver; thorns shall be in their tents.

Those who fled the Assyrian destruction by running to Egypt would not escape. Memphis, a great Egyptian city famous for its tombs, would bury them. Back home, weeds would grow over their treasures and thorns in their abandoned homes.

The days of punishment have come; the days of recompense have come; Israel shall know it. The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad, because of your great iniquity and great hatred.

The days of punishment have come. And the people's response to Hosea? The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad. They called him crazy. When God's messenger tells people what they do not want to hear, they often attack the messenger. The Roman governor Festus said the same to Paul: Paul, you are out of your mind (Acts 26:24). Their mockery showed the depth of their great hatred toward God.

The prophet is the watchman of Ephraim with my God; yet a fowler's snare is on all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God.

Hosea was not mad. He was a watchman, set by God on the wall to warn of danger, as God later told Ezekiel: I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel (Ezek 3:17). But instead of thanking the watchman, the people set traps for him and hated him even in the place of worship.

They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah: he will remember their iniquity; he will punish their sins.

The days of Gibeah recalls one of the darkest stories in Israel's history, told at the end of Judges. In Gibeah, a Levite's concubine was abused and murdered, and the crime led to a civil war that nearly destroyed the tribe of Benjamin. People said, Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt (Judg 19:30). Hosea says Israel had sunk to that level again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Like the Thing They Loved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel, but at Baal-peor they ... became detestable like the thing they loved (v. 10). Ephraim's glory will fly away, with no children (vv. 11-14). At Gilgal God began to hate them for their wickedness (v. 15). Ephraim is stricken and fruitless (v. 16); they shall be wanderers among the nations (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: We become like what we love; God's delight in his people turns to judgment when they give their love to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel. Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers. But they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved. Ephraim's glory shall fly away like a bird— no birth, no pregnancy, no conception! Even if they bring up children, I will bereave them till none is left. Woe to them when I depart from them! Ephraim, as I have seen, was like a young palm planted in a meadow; but Ephraim must lead his children out to slaughter. Give them, O LORD— what will you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel. Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers. But they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved.

Listen to God's memory of Israel's beginning. Finding grapes in the wilderness would be a thirsty traveler's delight, a surprise of sweetness in a barren place. The first fruit on the fig tree was the most prized fig of the year. That is how God felt about Israel when he first chose them. He delighted in them.

But they came to Baal-peor. Before they had even entered the promised land, Israel joined the Moabites in worshipping the god Baal of Peor, with sexual immorality and idol feasts (Num 25:1-3). They consecrated themselves to the thing of shame.

And then comes a profound truth: they became detestable like the thing they loved. We become like what we worship. Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them (Ps 115:8). If we love money, we become cold and grasping. If we love approval, we become hollow. If we love the true God, we are transformed into his likeness. Worship always shapes the worshipper.

Ephraim's glory shall fly away like a bird— no birth, no pregnancy, no conception!

Even if they bring up children, I will bereave them till none is left. Woe to them when I depart from them!

The judgment strikes at exactly what they had sought from Baal: fertility and children. Their glory, the growth of the nation, would fly away like a bird. And the worst woe is this: Woe to them when I depart from them! Losing children was terrible. Losing God was worse.

Ephraim, as I have seen, was like a young palm planted in a meadow; but Ephraim must lead his children out to slaughter.

Israel had been planted by God in a good place, like a young palm tree. Now its children would be led to slaughter. (The ESV notes an alternative reading, "like Tyre", and that to slaughter is literally "to him who slaughters".)

Give them, O LORD— what will you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.

Hosea interrupts with a prayer, and it is a hard one. He begins to ask God to give them something, and stops: what will you give? Then he asks for a miscarrying womb and dry breasts. Some understand this as a prayer for the lesser judgment. If children are only going to be born to be slaughtered, it would be kinder if they were never born. Jesus spoke in a similar way about the coming destruction of Jerusalem: Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore (Luke 23:29). Others read it as the anguished cry of a prophet who has come to agree with God's verdict. Either way, it shows how terrible the coming judgment was.

verseByVerse.quote: Every evil of theirs is in Gilgal; there I began to hate them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of my house. I will love them no more; all their princes are rebels. Ephraim is stricken; their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, I will put their beloved children to death. My God will reject them because they have not listened to him; they shall be wanderers among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every evil of theirs is in Gilgal; there I began to hate them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of my house. I will love them no more; all their princes are rebels.

Gilgal was a center of corrupt worship (4:15). It may also be mentioned because it was where Israel first made Saul king (1 Sam 11:15), the beginning of the monarchy that had led them so far astray. There I began to hate them.

These are some of the hardest words in the book: I will love them no more. They are the language of a husband driving an unfaithful wife out of my house. God's holy hatred of sin is real, and those who persist in rebellion face his rejection. Yet the book does not end here. In chapter 11 God will cry, How can I give you up, O Ephraim? (11:8), and in chapter 14 he will promise, I will love them freely (14:4). Hosea holds both truths together: God's wrath against sin is real, and his love is greater still. Those two truths meet at the cross, where God's judgment on sin and his love for sinners were both fully shown.

Ephraim is stricken; their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, I will put their beloved children to death.

The palm tree of verse 13 withers: their root is dried up. Israel's very name Ephraim was linked with fruitfulness (Gen 41:52), and now it would bear no fruit.

My God will reject them because they have not listened to him; they shall be wanderers among the nations.

Notice that Hosea says My God. Israel had abandoned God, but Hosea had not. And he gives the reason for the judgment in a few words: they have not listened to him. The result is exile: wanderers among the nations, like Cain, who became a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth (Gen 4:12). The northern tribes were scattered by Assyria and never returned as a nation.

But God's final word is not wandering. The same God who scatters in judgment would one day send his Son to seek and gather wanderers from every nation into one flock.

9.title: Grapes in the Wilderness
9.overview:
Israel must not rejoice like the nations, for it has played the whore and loved a prostitute's wages on the threshing floors. The harvest will fail; they will not remain in the LORD's land but return to Egypt and eat unclean food in Assyria, where their offerings will be like mourners' bread. What will they do on the festival day? Those who flee will be buried in Memphis, and weeds will cover their treasures (vv. 1-6).

The days of punishment have come. The people call the prophet a fool and a madman, though he is Ephraim's watchman with God; they set snares for him and hate him in God's house. They have corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah, and God will punish their sins (vv. 7-9).

God found Israel like grapes in the wilderness and the first figs, but at Baal-peor they consecrated themselves to shame and became detestable like what they loved. Ephraim's glory will fly away, with no birth or conception, and children will be bereaved. Hosea prays that God would give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts (vv. 10-14).

All their evil is at Gilgal, where God began to hate them; he will drive them from his house and love them no more. Ephraim is stricken and fruitless. God will reject them because they have not listened, and they will be wanderers among the nations (vv. 15-17).
9.theology:
The land and the feasts belong to the LORD, and those who give his gifts to idols will lose both (vv. 1-6).

People who reject God's word often mock his messengers, but the prophet is a watchman whose warnings are true (vv. 7-8; Acts 26:24; Ezek 3:17).

God delighted in his people from the beginning, yet they turned quickly to idols (v. 10; Num 25:1-3).

We become like what we love and worship (v. 10; Ps 115:8).

The worst judgment is God's departure from his people (v. 12).

God's holy rejection of persistent sin is real, yet his love proves greater, as the rest of Hosea shows and the cross reveals (vv. 15-17; 11:8; 14:4).
9.examples:
A harvest party interrupted by a prophet.

Meals eaten for hunger only, with nothing offered to God.

A watchman called a madman.

Grapes found in the wilderness.

People who became as shameful as the idol they loved.

A prophet who cannot finish his prayer for blessing.

A nation scattered as wanderers.
