verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The More His Fruit Increased
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is a luxuriant vine, but the more it prospered, the more altars it built (v. 1). Their heart is false, and God will destroy their altars (v. 2). They say, We have no king, for we do not fear the LORD, and they make empty covenants (vv. 3-4). The calf of Beth-aven will be carried to Assyria, and Samaria's king will perish like a twig on the water (vv. 5-7). The people will say to the mountains, Cover us, and to the hills, Fall on us (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: Prosperity that feeds idolatry ends in the loss of every false security.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit. The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built; as his country improved, he improved his pillars. Their heart is false; now they must bear their guilt. The LORD will break down their altars and destroy their pillars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit. The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built; as his country improved, he improved his pillars.

God had planted Israel as his vine, and it grew rich. But notice what the prosperity produced: The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built. Every rise in wealth became a rise in idolatry. The richer they got, the more they spent on pagan pillars, the sacred stones of Baal worship.

Prosperity is a test. God gives good things so that we will love him more. But our hearts are prone to take the gifts and use them to serve something else. Isaiah recorded God's disappointment over his vineyard: When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes? (Isa 5:4). Only one Vine has ever borne the fruit God desired, and Jesus says, I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit (John 15:5).

Their heart is false; now they must bear their guilt. The LORD will break down their altars and destroy their pillars.

Their heart is false, divided and deceitful. They wanted God's blessings and Baal's too. (The ESV notes that the second part of the verse literally says "He" will break down the altars.) God would destroy the altars they built with his gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: For now they will say: "We have no king, for we do not fear the LORD; and a king—what could he do for us?" They utter mere words; with empty oaths they make covenants; so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now they will say: "We have no king, for we do not fear the LORD; and a king—what could he do for us?"

The day would come when Israel would have no king at all. The last king, Hoshea, was taken prisoner by Assyria (2 Kgs 17:4), and the monarchy ended. And the people would finally see the connection: we have no king, for we do not fear the LORD. Then they would add, bitterly, a king—what could he do for us? They had trusted in their kings. Now they saw that no king could save them.

They utter mere words; with empty oaths they make covenants; so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field.

Their promises meant nothing. They swore oaths and broke them. (The ESV notes that empty may be "vain", pointing to the command not to take God's name in vain, Exod 20:7.) And the result was that justice itself became poisonous. Courts and agreements that should have protected people spread harm, like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field.

verseByVerse.quote: The inhabitants of Samaria tremble for the calf of Beth-aven. Its people mourn for it, and so do its idolatrous priests— those who rejoiced over it and over its glory— for it has departed from them. The thing itself shall be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king. Ephraim shall be put to shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his idol. Samaria's king shall perish like a twig on the face of the waters. The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed. Thorn and thistle shall grow up on their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, "Cover us," and to the hills, "Fall on us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The inhabitants of Samaria tremble for the calf of Beth-aven. Its people mourn for it, and so do its idolatrous priests— those who rejoiced over it and over its glory— for it has departed from them.

Here is something almost comic. The people tremble for their god. Instead of the god protecting the people, the people are afraid for the god. The golden calf at Bethel (here called Beth-aven, as in 4:15) is about to be carried off, and its worshippers and priests are mourning. (The ESV notes that calf may be "calves", and that departed may mean "gone into exile".) What kind of god has to be protected by its worshippers?

The thing itself shall be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king. Ephraim shall be put to shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his idol.

The golden calf would end up as a gift to the Assyrian king, loaded on a cart. (The ESV notes that the great king may be a name, "King Jareb", and that idol may be "counsel".) The object they worshipped would become loot. Every idol eventually shames those who trust it.

Samaria's king shall perish like a twig on the face of the waters.

The king would be swept away as helplessly as a twig in a flood.

The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed. Thorn and thistle shall grow up on their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, "Cover us," and to the hills, "Fall on us."

Weeds would grow over the altars. And the people would be so terrified that they would beg the mountains to fall on them and hide them. Jesus used these very words as he carried his cross to Golgotha, warning the women of Jerusalem about the judgment coming on their city: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, 'Fall on us,' and to the hills, 'Cover us' (Luke 23:30). And Revelation describes people at the final judgment calling to the mountains to hide them from the wrath of the Lamb (Rev 6:16). There is no hiding place from God except in the one who took that wrath for us.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah, and war will overtake them (vv. 9-10). The calf that loved easy threshing must take the yoke (v. 11). Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you (v. 12). But You have plowed iniquity; you have reaped injustice, trusting in warriors (v. 13), so war will destroy their fortresses, and the king of Israel will be cut off (vv. 14-15).
verseByVerse.theology: It is time to seek the LORD, breaking up hard hearts so that he may rain righteousness on us.

verseByVerse.quote: From the days of Gibeah, you have sinned, O Israel; there they have continued. Shall not the war against the unjust overtake them in Gibeah? When I please, I will discipline them, and nations shall be gathered against them when they are bound up for their double iniquity. Ephraim was a trained calf that loved to thresh, and I spared her fair neck; but I will put Ephraim to the yoke; Judah must plow; Jacob must harrow for himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the days of Gibeah, you have sinned, O Israel; there they have continued. Shall not the war against the unjust overtake them in Gibeah?

Hosea again recalls the days of Gibeah (9:9), when the terrible crime there led to war. Israel's sin was not new. It had been going on for centuries. And just as war came to Gibeah then, it would come again. (The ESV notes that the unjust is literally "the children of injustice".)

When I please, I will discipline them, and nations shall be gathered against them when they are bound up for their double iniquity.

God will choose the time. The nations will be his instruments. Double iniquity may refer to Israel's two great sins, idolatry and rebellion against God's appointed king, or simply to sin piled on sin.

Ephraim was a trained calf that loved to thresh, and I spared her fair neck; but I will put Ephraim to the yoke; Judah must plow; Jacob must harrow for himself.

A young cow used for threshing had an easy job. It walked in circles over the grain, and it was allowed to eat as it worked, for God's law said, You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain (Deut 25:4). Israel had enjoyed that kind of easy life. Now it would be put under a heavy yoke to plow the hard ground. Judah and all of Jacob's descendants would face hard labor too. The easy days were over.

verseByVerse.quote: Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you.

In the middle of the judgment comes one of the most beautiful invitations in Hosea. Using the picture of farming, God calls his people to a new way of life.

Sow for yourselves righteousness. Plant good seed: justice, honesty and obedience. Reap steadfast love. The harvest will be God's covenant love. Break up your fallow ground. Fallow ground is a field left unplowed so long that the soil has become hard and crusted. Nothing can grow there until the plow breaks it open. Jeremiah used the same words: Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns (Jer 4:3). Israel's heart had become like that hard field. It needed to be broken up by repentance.

For it is the time to seek the LORD. Not tomorrow. Now. And the promise is wonderful: that he may come and rain righteousness upon you. Israel sought rain from Baal. God promises to rain righteousness itself. We do the plowing and sowing, but only God can send the rain that makes anything grow.

For the Christian, this is exactly what the gospel does. Christ comes and pours out righteousness on hard hearts that are broken open in repentance. Whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully (2 Cor 9:6), and Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy! (Ps 126:5).

verseByVerse.quote: You have plowed iniquity; you have reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors, therefore the tumult of war shall arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be destroyed, as Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel on the day of battle; mothers were dashed in pieces with their children. Thus it shall be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great evil. At dawn the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You have plowed iniquity; you have reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors,

But Israel had done the opposite of verse 12. They plowed iniquity and harvested injustice, and they were now eating the fruit of lies. The root of it all: you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors. Self-reliance and military strength were their gods.

therefore the tumult of war shall arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be destroyed, as Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel on the day of battle; mothers were dashed in pieces with their children.

The warriors they trusted would not save the fortresses. Hosea points to a massacre his hearers knew well: Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel. We no longer know exactly which event this was. Some think Shalman was the Assyrian king Shalmaneser, others a Moabite king. But the horror was clear: mothers and children killed together. The same would happen to Israel.

Thus it shall be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great evil. At dawn the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off.

Bethel was the place where Jacob met God and said, This is none other than the house of God (Gen 28:17). It had become the home of the golden calf. Now it would bring destruction on the nation. And at dawn, as suddenly as the sun rises, the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off. This was probably fulfilled when Hoshea, Israel's last king, was captured by Assyria.

The chapter holds out two harvests. One is righteousness and steadfast love, rained down by God on those who seek him. The other is war and destruction for those who trust their own way. The field is still before every reader. It is the time to seek the LORD.

10.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
10.overview:
Israel is a luxuriant vine, but as its fruit and prosperity increased, it multiplied altars and pillars. Their heart is false, and God will break down their altars. They will say they have no king because they did not fear the LORD, and what could a king do? They speak empty words and make false covenants, so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds (vv. 1-4).

Samaria trembles for the calf of Beth-aven, which will be carried to Assyria as tribute; Israel will be ashamed of its idol, and its king will perish like a twig on the water. The high places will be destroyed and overgrown, and the people will beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them (vv. 5-8).

Israel has sinned since the days of Gibeah, and war will overtake them; God will discipline them when nations gather against them. Ephraim, a trained heifer that loved to thresh, will be put to the yoke. Israel is called to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love and break up its fallow ground, for it is time to seek the LORD, that he may rain righteousness on them. But they have plowed iniquity, reaped injustice and eaten the fruit of lies, trusting their own way and their warriors, so war will destroy their fortresses as Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel, and at dawn Israel's king will be cut off (vv. 9-15).
10.theology:
Prosperity that is not received with gratitude to God becomes fuel for idolatry (v. 1; Isa 5:4).

Only Christ, the true vine, bears the fruit God desires, and those who abide in him bear fruit (v. 1; John 15:5).

Idols must be protected by their worshippers and finally shame them (vv. 5-6).

There is no hiding place from God's judgment except in the one who bore it (v. 8; Luke 23:30; Rev 6:16).

Now is the time to seek the LORD: hard hearts must be broken up in repentance so that God may rain righteousness upon them (v. 12; Jer 4:3; 2 Cor 9:6; Ps 126:5).

Those who plow iniquity and trust in their own strength reap destruction (vv. 13-15; Gal 6:7-8).
10.examples:
A vine that grows richer and builds more altars.

A king who could do nothing for his people.

Worshippers trembling for the safety of their god.

A golden calf loaded on a cart as tribute.

People begging the mountains to fall on them.

A hard, crusted field waiting for the plow.

Rain of righteousness on broken ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — When Israel Was a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son (v. 1). But the more God called, the more they went after the Baals (v. 2). Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; God led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, bent down and fed them (vv. 3-4). Because they refused to return, Assyria will be their king and the sword will rage in their cities (vv. 5-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love for his people is the love of a father who carried, taught and fed a child who turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.

Chapter 11 is one of the tenderest passages in the Old Testament. Until now Hosea has mostly pictured God as a husband betrayed by his wife. Here God speaks as a father remembering his child.

When Israel was a child, I loved him. God's love came first. Israel had done nothing to earn it. When Israel was still a slave nation in Egypt, weak and insignificant, God loved him. Moses told Pharaoh, Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son... Let my son go (Exod 4:22-23). And God did bring his son out: out of Egypt I called my son.

Matthew quotes this verse in a surprising place. When Joseph took the baby Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod and later brought him back, Matthew writes, This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son" (Matt 2:15).

Some readers object that Hosea was looking back to the exodus, not forward to Jesus. That is true, and Matthew knew it. Matthew is not saying Hosea predicted a trip to Egypt. He is saying that Jesus is the true Son of God, who lived out Israel's story in his own life, and lived it faithfully. Israel, God's son, came out of Egypt and then turned away (v. 2). Jesus, God's Son, came out of Egypt and never turned away. Israel was tested in the wilderness and failed. Jesus was tested in the wilderness and did not fail. Where Israel the son broke his Father's heart, Jesus the Son did always what pleased his Father. The story of Israel reaches its fulfilment in him.

verseByVerse.quote: The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols. Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them. I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, and I became to them as one who eases the yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols.

Here is the tragedy. The more they were called, the more they went away. God kept calling through Moses, the judges and the prophets, and every call was answered by running further away, toward the Baals. It is like a parent calling a child home, and the child running faster in the other direction every time.

Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them.

Now God remembers the little things a parent does. It was I who taught Ephraim to walk. Picture a father holding a toddler's hands, lifting the child when he stumbles, taking him up by their arms. Moses had said the same: in the wilderness the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son (Deut 1:31).

And the heartbreaking line: they did not know that I healed them. Like children who take their parents' care for granted, Israel never realized how much God had done for them. We rarely know how many times God has picked us up, healed us and kept us.

I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, and I became to them as one who eases the yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them.

God did not drive his people like cattle. He led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love. (The ESV notes that kindness may be "humaneness", literally cords of a "man": the kind of ties by which one person draws another, not ropes for animals.) He was like a farmer who lifts the yoke off an ox's neck so it can eat, and bent down to them and fed them. The God of heaven stooped down to feed his children.

That picture of God bending down reaches its fullest meaning in the incarnation. In Christ, God did not only bend down. He came all the way down, took our flesh and fed us with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Assyria shall be their king, because they have refused to return to me. The sword shall rage against their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them because of their own counsels. My people are bent on turning away from me, and though they call out to the Most High, he shall not raise them up at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Assyria shall be their king, because they have refused to return to me.

This verse can seem to contradict earlier warnings that Israel would return to Egypt (8:13; 9:3). The ESV notes that it may be read "surely" they shall return to Egypt. Either way, the main point is clear. Their real master would be Assyria, because they have refused to return to me. Notice the play on the word return. They would not return to God, so they would be carried off into captivity. Those who will not return to the Lord will be taken where they do not want to go.

The sword shall rage against their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them because of their own counsels.

Their own plans, their counsels, would destroy them. Every scheme they trusted instead of God would bring the sword.

My people are bent on turning away from me, and though they call out to the Most High, he shall not raise them up at all.

My people. Even now God calls them his. But they are bent on turning away, determined, set in their course. Calling on God with their lips while their hearts are set on leaving him would not save them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — My Heart Recoils Within Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? God will not make them like Admah and Zeboiim: My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender (v. 8). I will not execute my burning anger ... for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst (v. 9). When the LORD roars like a lion, his children will come trembling home from Egypt and Assyria (vv. 10-11). Yet Ephraim surrounds God with lies (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's holy compassion will not let his people go, and his mercy triumphs over the judgment they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.

Now we hear something astonishing: God arguing with himself. After all the charges, after all the sentences of judgment, God cries out: How can I give you up, O Ephraim?

Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah, which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath (Deut 29:23). They were wiped out completely, never to rise again. Israel deserved the same. But God cannot bring himself to do it. My heart recoils within me. The picture is of a heart in turmoil. My compassion grows warm and tender.

This is not weakness in God. It is the deep, passionate love of a Father who will not let his child go. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps 103:13). Jesus showed the same heart when he wept over Jerusalem: How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings (Luke 13:34).

I will not execute my burning anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath.

Why will God not destroy them completely? For I am God and not a man. A human being who had been betrayed like this would give up. A man would say, "Enough." God's love is not like ours. It does not run out. And notice how God describes himself: the Holy One in your midst. We might expect God's holiness to be the reason he destroys them. Instead, his holiness is the reason he does not. God's holiness is not only his purity, but his utter difference from us, including the difference of his mercy. (The ESV notes that the final phrase may be "I will not come into the city".)

How does this fit with the rest of the book, which warns that Israel will fall? The northern kingdom did fall to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kgs 17). Judgment came. But God did not make them like Admah, wiped out without a future. He preserved a people and promised to bring them home.

And there is a deeper answer. God's anger against sin is real, and it must go somewhere. In the end, God did not simply decide to overlook Israel's sin, or ours. He poured out his burning anger on his own Son, the true Israel who came out of Egypt. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32). "How can I give you up?" God asked of Israel. At the cross, he gave up his Son, so that he would never have to give up his people.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall go after the LORD; he will roar like a lion; when he roars, his children shall come trembling from the west; they shall come trembling like birds from Egypt, and like doves from the land of Assyria, and I will return them to their homes, declares the LORD. Ephraim has surrounded me with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit, but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They shall go after the LORD; he will roar like a lion; when he roars, his children shall come trembling from the west;

The lion appears again, but this time the roar is not a threat. It is a call home. In 5:14 God was a lion who tore his people. Here he is a lion whose roar gathers his children. They will go after the LORD, following him instead of running away, and come trembling, with reverent awe, from the far places where they were scattered.

they shall come trembling like birds from Egypt, and like doves from the land of Assyria, and I will return them to their homes, declares the LORD.

In 7:11 Ephraim was like a dove, silly and without sense, flying to Egypt and Assyria for help. Now the same doves fly back home from Egypt and Assyria, returning to God. Isaiah foresaw the same great homecoming: the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt (Isa 11:11). God's final purpose is not scattering but gathering, and in Christ he is gathering his children from every nation.

Ephraim has surrounded me with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit, but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.

(The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 12.) After the promise, the prophet returns to present reality. Ephraim still surrounds God with lies. But for the moment, Judah still walks with God. The contrast serves as both a rebuke to Israel and a warning to Judah to remain faithful.

Chapter 11 shows us the heart behind the whole book. All the warnings, all the judgments, all the pleading come from a Father's love. How can I give you up? That question is answered finally in the gospel. God will not give up his people, because he gave up his Son for them.

11.title: How Can I Give You Up?
11.overview:
God loved Israel when he was a child and called his son out of Egypt, but the more he called, the more they went after the Baals and idols. God taught Ephraim to walk, took them in his arms, healed them, led them with cords of kindness and bands of love, eased their yoke and bent down to feed them. Because they refused to return, they will not go back to Egypt but Assyria will rule them; the sword will rage in their cities because of their schemes. God's people are bent on turning away, and though they call to the Most High, he will not raise them up (vv. 1-7).

God cries out, "How can I give you up, O Ephraim?" He cannot make them like Admah and Zeboiim; his heart recoils and his compassion grows warm. He will not execute his burning anger or destroy Ephraim again, for he is God and not a man, the Holy One in their midst. They will follow the LORD, who will roar like a lion, and his children will come trembling from the west, from Egypt and Assyria like birds and doves, and he will return them to their homes. Yet Ephraim surrounds God with lies, while Judah still walks with God (vv. 8-12).
11.theology:
God's love for his people is prior, undeserved and fatherly (vv. 1, 3-4; Exod 4:22-23; Deut 1:31; Ps 103:13).

Jesus is the true Son of God who relived Israel's story and remained faithful where Israel failed (v. 1; Matt 2:15).

God's people often do not realize how much he has carried, healed and fed them (vv. 3-4).

Those who refuse to return to God are carried where they do not want to go (vv. 5-7).

God's holy compassion will not let his people go; he is God and not man, and his mercy triumphs over the judgment they deserve (vv. 8-9; Luke 13:34).

God did not give up his people because he gave up his own Son for them (vv. 8-9; Rom 8:32).

God's final purpose is to gather his scattered children home (vv. 10-11; Isa 11:11).
11.examples:
A father teaching a toddler to walk.

A child who runs faster the more he is called.

Cords of kindness instead of ropes for cattle.

The God of heaven bending down to feed his children.

A heart that recoils at the thought of destroying its child.

A lion's roar that calls children home.

Doves flying back from Egypt and Assyria.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim feeds on the wind, making covenants with Assyria and sending oil to Egypt (v. 1). The LORD brings a charge against Judah and Jacob (v. 2). In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God; he wept, sought God's favor and met him at Bethel (vv. 3-5). So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who met and changed Jacob still calls his descendants to return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; they multiply falsehood and violence; they make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried to Egypt. The LORD has an indictment against Judah and will punish Jacob according to his ways; he will repay him according to his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; they multiply falsehood and violence; they make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried to Egypt.

Ephraim feeds on the wind. Imagine trying to fill your stomach by eating air. And not just any wind, but the east wind, the scorching wind off the desert that withered crops. Israel's policies were exactly that: empty and destructive. They made a covenant with Assyria while sending oil, a valuable gift, to Egypt, trying to keep both superpowers happy. It was the same double-dealing that finally ruined King Hoshea (2 Kgs 17:4).

The LORD has an indictment against Judah and will punish Jacob according to his ways; he will repay him according to his deeds.

Judah is included too. Jacob here means the whole people descended from Jacob, and it introduces what follows. Hosea is about to tell Jacob's own story as a mirror for his descendants.

verseByVerse.quote: In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God. He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us— the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is his memorial name: "So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God.

Hosea goes back to the beginning. Jacob, the father of the nation, was a grasper from birth. When the twins were born, Jacob came out holding Esau's heel (Gen 25:26). All his life he schemed to get ahead, cheating his brother and his father. His descendants were acting just like him, grasping for wealth and security by deceit.

But Jacob's story did not end there. In his manhood he strove with God. On the night before he met Esau, alone by the river Jabbok, Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man and would not let go: I will not let you go unless you bless me. And God gave him a new name: Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed (Gen 32:26, 28).

He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us—

Notice how Hosea describes that wrestling match. Jacob prevailed, but how? He wept and sought his favor. Jacob won by weeping, by clinging to God and begging for his blessing. His strength was broken, and in his weakness he received grace. (The ESV notes that He met God is literally "He met him".)

And He met God at Bethel, the place where he first saw the stairway to heaven and said, This is none other than the house of God (Gen 28:17), and where God later renewed his name Israel (Gen 35:9-10). Then Hosea says something remarkable: there God spoke with us. What God said to Jacob, he said to all Jacob's children. The story of their ancestor is their story too.

The point is this. Israel had become Jacob the grasper again. But the God who changed Jacob could change them. The way back was the way Jacob found: weeping, clinging to God and seeking his favor. The same is true for us. God does not bless the strong who grasp. He blesses the broken who cling to him.

the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is his memorial name:

This is the God they are dealing with: the LORD, the God of hosts, the commander of heaven's armies. The LORD is his memorial name, the name he gave Moses at the burning bush: This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations (Exod 3:15). The God of Jacob is the same God still.

"So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God."

Here is the application, and it is a complete description of the life of faith in one sentence. First, by the help of your God. They cannot do it in their own strength, any more than Jacob could. Second, return. Turn back to God. Third, hold fast to love and justice, the loyal love and fair dealing that were missing in the land (4:1). Fourth, wait continually for your God. Not scheming, not running to Assyria or Egypt, but trusting and waiting.

Waiting for God is one of the hardest disciplines of faith. Jacob spent his early life refusing to wait, grabbing what God had promised him anyway. The life of faith is learning to wait continually for God to act.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — I Am the LORD Your God from the Land of Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim is a merchant with false balances who boasts, Ah, but I am rich, and thinks no one can find sin in him (vv. 7-8). But God, their God since Egypt, will make them live in tents again (v. 9). He spoke through prophets (v. 10); Gilead and Gilgal will come to nothing (v. 11). Jacob served for a wife, and By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt (vv. 12-13). Ephraim has bitterly provoked God and will bear his guilt (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Self-satisfied prosperity blinds people to their sin, but God's word through his prophets calls them back.

verseByVerse.quote: A merchant, in whose hands are false balances, he loves to oppress. Ephraim has said, "Ah, but I am rich; I have found wealth for myself; in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin." I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A merchant, in whose hands are false balances, he loves to oppress.

But Israel was not holding fast to justice. It was like a crooked merchant with rigged scales, cheating customers and loving it. A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight (Prov 11:1). Jacob the cheater lived on in his children.

Ephraim has said, "Ah, but I am rich; I have found wealth for myself; in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin."

Listen to Ephraim's boast. I am rich; I have found wealth for myself. He takes the credit. And he adds: they cannot find in me iniquity or sin. In other words, "My business is legal. No one can prove I did anything wrong." Wealth had blinded him to his own sin. The risen Christ said the same to the church in Laodicea: For you say, "I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing," not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked (Rev 3:17). Prosperity is one of the most effective blindfolds there is.

I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.

God answers the boast by reminding them who he is: the LORD your God from the land of Egypt. Everything they had came from the God who rescued them from slavery. And he would take them back to where they started: dwell in tents. Every year at the Feast of Booths, Israel lived in simple shelters for a week to remember that God had brought them through the wilderness (Lev 23:42-43). Now the whole nation would lose its houses and live that way again. It was a judgment, but also a chance to start over, as in the wilderness of 2:14.

verseByVerse.quote: I spoke to the prophets; it was I who multiplied visions, and through the prophets gave parables. If there is iniquity in Gilead, they shall surely come to nothing: in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars also are like stone heaps on the furrows of the field. Jacob fled to the land of Aram; there Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded sheep. By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt, and by a prophet he was guarded. Ephraim has given bitter provocation; so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt on him and will repay him for his disgraceful deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I spoke to the prophets; it was I who multiplied visions, and through the prophets gave parables.

God had not been silent. He had spoken through prophet after prophet, with visions and parables. Hosea's own marriage was a living parable. Israel could never say that God had not warned them.

If there is iniquity in Gilead, they shall surely come to nothing: in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars also are like stone heaps on the furrows of the field.

Gilead, east of the Jordan, was full of iniquity (6:8). Gilgal, west of the Jordan, was full of false sacrifices (4:15; 9:15). Their many altars would be reduced to piles of stones, like the heaps of rocks a farmer clears from his field.

Jacob fled to the land of Aram; there Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded sheep.

Hosea returns to Jacob's story. After cheating Esau, Jacob had to run for his life to Aram, where he worked as a shepherd for years to win Rachel. So Jacob served seven years for Rachel (Gen 29:20). The proud ancestor of the nation began as a fugitive and a hired hand. Israel had no reason for pride. Everything they became was by God's grace.

By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt, and by a prophet he was guarded.

Notice the contrast. Jacob guarded sheep for a wife (v. 12). But God guarded Israel by a prophet, Moses, who led them out of Egypt and through the wilderness. God saved his people not through their cleverness but through his word, spoken by his prophet.

Moses had promised that God would raise up a prophet like me from among you (Deut 18:15), and Peter declared that this prophet is Jesus (Acts 3:22). God's people are still brought out of slavery and guarded on the way home by a Prophet: the Lord Jesus Christ, who is himself God's final word.

Ephraim has given bitter provocation; so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt on him and will repay him for his disgraceful deeds.

But Ephraim had ignored the prophets and provoked God bitterly. So the guilt of the blood they had shed would remain on them. Those who refuse the Prophet God sends must carry their own guilt. Those who receive him find their guilt carried away.

12.title: Return and Wait for Your God
12.overview:
Ephraim feeds on the wind, multiplying falsehood and violence, making a covenant with Assyria and sending oil to Egypt. The LORD brings an indictment against Judah and will punish Jacob according to his deeds (vv. 1-2).

In the womb Jacob took his brother by the heel, and as a man he strove with God. He struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, where God spoke with us: the LORD, the God of hosts, whose memorial name is the LORD. So Israel is to return by God's help, hold fast to love and justice and wait continually for God (vv. 3-6).

Ephraim is a merchant with false balances who loves to oppress, and boasts that he is rich and that no one can find sin in his labors. But the LORD, their God from Egypt, will make them dwell in tents again as in the days of the feast. He spoke through the prophets with visions and parables. Gilead is full of iniquity, and the altars of Gilgal will become heaps of stones (vv. 7-11).

Jacob fled to Aram and served as a shepherd for a wife, but by a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt and guarded him. Ephraim has bitterly provoked God, who will leave his bloodguilt on him and repay his disgraceful deeds (vv. 12-14).
12.theology:
Seeking security through worldly alliances is feeding on the wind (v. 1).

God changed Jacob the grasper through wrestling, weeping and seeking his favor, and he still blesses the broken who cling to him (vv. 3-4; Gen 32:24-28).

The life of faith is returning to God by his help, holding fast to love and justice, and waiting continually for him (v. 6).

Dishonest gain and self-satisfied wealth blind people to their sin (vv. 7-8; Prov 11:1; Rev 3:17).

God speaks to his people through his prophets, and he saves and guards them by his word, fulfilled in Jesus the Prophet like Moses (vv. 10, 13; Deut 18:15; Acts 3:22).

Those who refuse God's word bear their own guilt (v. 14).
12.examples:
A nation trying to fill its stomach with the desert wind.

A baby grabbing his twin's heel.

A man who won a wrestling match by weeping.

A merchant who says, "No one can prove I did anything wrong."

A rich nation sent back to live in tents.

A shepherd guarding sheep, and a prophet guarding a nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Besides Me There Is No Savior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim was once exalted but died through Baal, and now they make more idols and kiss calves (vv. 1-2), so they will vanish like morning mist, chaff and smoke (v. 3). But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; you know no God but me, and besides me there is no savior (v. 4). God cared for them in the wilderness, but when they had grazed, they became full ... therefore they forgot me (vv. 5-6). So God will be to them like a lion, a leopard and a bear robbed of her cubs, for Israel is against your helper (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no savior but the LORD, and those who forget him in their fullness meet him as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died. And now they sin more and more, and make for themselves metal images, idols skillfully made of their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen. It is said of them, "Those who offer human sacrifice kiss calves!" Therefore they shall be like the morning mist or like the dew that goes early away, like the chaff that swirls from the threshing floor or like smoke from a window.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died.

Ephraim was once the leading tribe of the north. The first king of the northern kingdom, Jeroboam, came from Ephraim, and when Ephraim spoke, there was trembling. Other tribes listened. But Ephraim incurred guilt through Baal and died. The moment they turned to Baal, they were spiritually dead, even though they went on living and prospering for a long time. Sin kills before it buries.

And now they sin more and more, and make for themselves metal images, idols skillfully made of their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen. It is said of them, "Those who offer human sacrifice kiss calves!"

Instead of repenting, they sin more and more. They make more idols, skillfully crafted, but still the work of craftsmen (8:6). And the saying that went around was shocking: Those who offer human sacrifice kiss calves! People who would offer their own children to false gods would bow down and kiss a metal calf. Kissing an idol was an act of worship and devotion (1 Kgs 19:18). The contrast is grotesque: love for a statue, cruelty to children.

Therefore they shall be like the morning mist or like the dew that goes early away, like the chaff that swirls from the threshing floor or like smoke from a window.

Four pictures of things that vanish. Morning mist and dew disappear when the sun rises. Chaff blows away in the wind. Smoke drifts out of a window and is gone. In 6:4, Israel's love was like mist and dew. Now Israel itself will be. Those who live for what does not last will not last either.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; you know no God but me, and besides me there is no savior. It was I who knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought; but when they had grazed, they became full, they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; you know no God but me, and besides me there is no savior.

Against all the vanishing things stands God. But I am the LORD your God. He has been their God since Egypt. He is the only God they have ever truly known, and besides me there is no savior. Isaiah says the same: I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior (Isa 43:11).

This is the exclusive claim of the Bible. There is only one Savior. Baal cannot save. Assyria cannot save. Money, armies and alliances cannot save. And the New Testament applies this truth to Jesus: there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). The only Savior of Israel has come in the flesh.

It was I who knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought;

God knew them, cared for them personally, in the hardest place, the land of drought. In the wilderness they had nothing, and God gave them manna, water and protection.

but when they had grazed, they became full, they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me.

Here is the pattern of every spiritual decline. In need, they depended on God. When they were full, their heart was lifted up, and therefore they forgot me. (The ESV notes that when they had grazed is literally "according to their pasture", like cattle growing fat.) Moses had warned about exactly this: lest, when you have eaten and are full... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God (Deut 8:12, 14). Hard times are dangerous. Good times may be more dangerous still.

verseByVerse.quote: So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way. I will fall upon them like a bear robbed of her cubs; I will tear open their breast, and there I will devour them like a lion, as a wild beast would rip them open. He destroys you, O Israel, for you are against me, against your helper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way.

I will fall upon them like a bear robbed of her cubs; I will tear open their breast, and there I will devour them like a lion, as a wild beast would rip them open.

The God who fed them like a shepherd in the wilderness now comes against them like the wild animals that attack a flock: a lion, a leopard lying in ambush, and most terrifying of all, a bear robbed of her cubs. These are hard words, but they are honest. The same God who is a Shepherd to those who trust him is a lion to those who forget him. God's love is not soft toward sin.

He destroys you, O Israel, for you are against me, against your helper.

Here is the tragic irony. Israel is destroyed because it turned against your helper. The one person who could help them was the one they opposed. (The ESV notes that the verse may be read "I will destroy you".) People who fight against God are fighting against the only help they have.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — I Shall Ransom Them from the Power of Sheol
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Where now is your king, to save you? (vv. 10-11). Ephraim's sin is stored up, and he is like an unwise child who will not be born (vv. 12-13). I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? (v. 14). But the east wind will come, and Samaria will fall by the sword (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Only God can deliver from death, and in Christ he has taken away death's sting.

verseByVerse.quote: Where now is your king, to save you in all your cities? Where are all your rulers— those of whom you said, "Give me a king and princes"? I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath. The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is kept in store. The pangs of childbirth come for him, but he is an unwise son, for at the right time he does not present himself at the opening of the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Where now is your king, to save you in all your cities? Where are all your rulers— those of whom you said, "Give me a king and princes"?

Where now is your king? Israel had put its trust in kings. The last king of the north was captured by Assyria. Where was he now, when they needed saving? The request Give me a king and princes recalls the day Israel demanded a king from Samuel. God told Samuel, they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam 8:7).

I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath.

This may refer to Saul, the first king, given when Israel rejected God's rule and later removed. Or it may describe the whole line of northern kings, who came and went in God's judgment. Either way, God gave them what they insisted on, and it did not save them. Sometimes the worst thing God can do is give people what they demand.

The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is kept in store.

Ephraim's sins are not forgotten. They are wrapped up and stored away, like documents kept for a trial. Every unforgiven sin is being kept for the day of reckoning.

The pangs of childbirth come for him, but he is an unwise son, for at the right time he does not present himself at the opening of the womb.

A striking picture. The labor pains have begun, the moment of birth has come, but the baby will not come out. It stays where it is, and both mother and child are in mortal danger. Israel was at the moment of crisis, the time when it should have been reborn through repentance, and it refused to move. Every crisis God sends is a moment when we may be born anew or refuse.

verseByVerse.quote: I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? Compassion is hidden from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? Compassion is hidden from my eyes.

This is one of the most famous and most debated verses in Hosea. Sheol is the Old Testament word for the grave, the realm of the dead.

The ESV notes that the first two lines may be translated as questions: "Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?" Read that way, the verse is a threat. God asks whether he should rescue Israel, and the answer is no. He calls on Death and Sheol to bring on their plagues and sting, and says, Compassion is hidden from my eyes. Many interpreters believe this fits the surrounding verses, which are full of judgment.

The ESV text, however, translates the lines as a promise: I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. Read this way, God interrupts the judgment to announce that he will conquer death itself, taunting it: O Death, where are your plagues? And Compassion is hidden from my eyes would then mean that God will not pity death, or that he will not change his mind about this promise.

The apostle Paul shows what this verse means for Christians. In his great chapter on the resurrection he quotes it as a shout of victory: "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor 15:55-57). Whatever the verse meant as a word of judgment on Israel in Hosea's day, God's final answer to it is resurrection.

Here is how the two readings come together. Death does have a sting, and its sting is sin. Israel deserved death, and so do we. But God himself paid the ransom. Christ, the true Israel, went down into death, bearing the sting of sin, so that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death... and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15). Our Savior abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10). For those who belong to him, death is a defeated enemy. We can stand at a grave and ask, O Death, where are your plagues?

verseByVerse.quote: Though he may flourish among his brothers, the east wind, the wind of the LORD, shall come, rising from the wilderness, and his fountain shall dry up; his spring shall be parched; it shall strip his treasury of every precious thing. Samaria shall bear her guilt, because she has rebelled against her God; they shall fall by the sword; their little ones shall be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though he may flourish among his brothers, the east wind, the wind of the LORD, shall come, rising from the wilderness, and his fountain shall dry up; his spring shall be parched; it shall strip his treasury of every precious thing.

Ephraim's name was connected with fruitfulness (Gen 41:52), and he could flourish among his brothers. But the scorching east wind from the desert would come, and it is called the wind of the LORD. Assyria, coming from the east, was God's instrument. Every source of life would dry up, and every treasure would be carried away.

Samaria shall bear her guilt, because she has rebelled against her God; they shall fall by the sword; their little ones shall be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open.

(The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 14:1.) The chapter ends with the horrors of ancient warfare. Invading armies really did such things (2 Kgs 8:12), and Assyria was notorious for cruelty. It is painful to read. Samaria would bear her guilt, because she has rebelled against her God.

We should not soften this verse. Sin is not a small matter, and rebellion against God has terrible consequences, which often fall on the innocent too. But the book does not end here. The next words are among the most hopeful in Hosea: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God (14:1). The God who stated the full horror of judgment is the God who still invites his people home. And the God who promised to ransom them from death has done it, in Jesus Christ.

13.title: O Death, Where Are Your Plagues?
13.overview:
When Ephraim spoke, others trembled, but he became guilty through Baal and died. They sin more and more, making idols of silver, the work of craftsmen, and people who offer human sacrifice kiss calves. So they will vanish like morning mist, dew, chaff and smoke (vv. 1-3).

The LORD has been their God since Egypt; they know no God but him, and besides him there is no savior. He knew them in the wilderness, but when they were full their hearts were lifted up and they forgot him. So he will be like a lion, a leopard and a bear robbed of her cubs, tearing them apart. Israel is destroyed because it is against its helper (vv. 4-9).

Where is their king to save them? God gave them a king in anger and took him away in wrath. Ephraim's iniquity is stored up; he is like an unwise child who will not come out at birth. God will ransom them from Sheol and redeem them from Death: "O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?" Though Ephraim flourishes, the east wind of the LORD will dry up his spring and strip his treasury, and Samaria will bear her guilt and fall by the sword (vv. 10-16).
13.theology:
Turning to idols brings spiritual death even while outward life goes on (vv. 1-2).

Those who live for what vanishes will vanish with it (v. 3).

There is no savior but the LORD, who has come in Jesus Christ (v. 4; Isa 43:11; Acts 4:12).

Fullness and prosperity can lead God's people to forget him (vv. 5-6; Deut 8:12-14).

The God who shepherds those who trust him comes as judge against those who oppose their only helper (vv. 7-9).

God may give people the kings they demand, and those kings cannot save (vv. 10-11; 1 Sam 8:7).

Death's sting is sin, but God has ransomed his people from death through the death and resurrection of Christ (v. 14; 1 Cor 15:55-57; Heb 2:14-15; 2 Tim 1:10).
13.examples:
A tribe that was dead long before it was buried.

People who kiss a metal calf and sacrifice their children.

Mist, dew, chaff and smoke.

Cattle that grow fat and forget the farmer.

A bear robbed of her cubs.

A baby who will not be born when the time comes.

A Christian at a graveside asking, "O Death, where is your sting?"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled because of your iniquity (v. 1). Take with you words and return to the LORD; say to him, "Take away all iniquity; accept what is good" (v. 2). They will renounce Assyria, horses and idols: In you the orphan finds mercy (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: True repentance brings honest words of confession, renounces every false savior and trusts God's mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled because of your iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled because of your iniquity.

After thirteen chapters of warnings and pleading, the book ends with an invitation. Return. It is the word Hosea has used again and again. Israel would not return (5:4; 7:10; 11:5). Now the call comes one last time.

Notice two things. First, God is still the LORD your God. After all their unfaithfulness, the relationship is not beyond repair. Second, the problem is named honestly: you have stumbled because of your iniquity. They did not fall because of bad luck, bad leaders or powerful enemies. They fell because of their own sin. Returning to God always begins with owning that.

verseByVerse.quote: Take with you words and return to the LORD; say to him, "Take away all iniquity; accept what is good, and we will pay with bulls the vows of our lips. Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, 'Our God,' to the work of our hands. In you the orphan finds mercy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take with you words and return to the LORD; say to him, "Take away all iniquity; accept what is good, and we will pay with bulls the vows of our lips.

Take with you words. Israel had brought God plenty of animals. God does not ask for more sacrifices. He asks for words, honest words of confession. God even gives them the words to say. That is grace. He not only invites us back, he teaches us how to pray.

The prayer begins, Take away all iniquity. Not some of it. All of it. Only God can do that. Then, accept what is good, receive us graciously. And, we will pay with bulls the vows of our lips. The ESV notes that the ancient Greek and Syriac translations read "pay the fruit of our lips". Their offering would now be praise. The New Testament uses the same idea: let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name (Heb 13:15).

Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, 'Our God,' to the work of our hands. In you the orphan finds mercy."

True repentance names and renounces its idols. And Israel renounces the three false saviors that Hosea has exposed throughout the book. Assyria shall not save us: no more trusting political alliances. We will not ride on horses: no more trusting military power. We will say no more, 'Our God,' to the work of our hands: no more idols.

Then comes the final line, and it is beautiful: In you the orphan finds mercy. An orphan has no one to protect or provide. Israel comes to God as a helpless orphan, with nothing to offer. And the word mercy takes us back to the beginning of the book, to the little girl named No Mercy (1:6). Those who were No Mercy find mercy in God.

This is how every sinner comes to God. We bring nothing but words of confession and empty hands. We give up every false savior. And we find mercy.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — I Will Be Like the Dew to Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them (v. 4). God will be like the dew, and Israel will blossom like the lily, take root like Lebanon's trees and spread like the olive and the vine (vv. 5-7). O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you. I am like an evergreen cypress; from me comes your fruit (v. 8). The ways of the LORD are right, and the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers repentance with free, healing love, and all his people's fruitfulness comes from him.

verseByVerse.quote: I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.

Now God answers the prayer, and his answer is overwhelming.

I will heal their apostasy. Their unfaithfulness, their constant turning away, is treated as a sickness God will heal. He does not only forgive past wandering. He cures the heart that wanders.

I will love them freely. This may be the best summary of the whole book. God's love is free: not earned, not deserved, not paid for by Israel, but given freely out of his own heart. In 9:15 God had said, I will love them no more. Now he says, I will love them freely. Nothing in Israel had changed to make them lovable. The change came from God. But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy (Titus 3:4-5).

For my anger has turned from them. God's anger was real. But it has turned away. How can a holy God turn his anger away from sinners? The Old Testament does not yet tell us fully. The New Testament does: God's anger was turned away because it fell on Christ, who bore it in our place. That is why believers can hear these words as spoken to them.

verseByVerse.quote: I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon; his shoots shall spread out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon. They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon;

In 6:4 Israel's love was like the dew that goes early away. In 13:3 Israel itself would vanish like dew. Now God says, I will be like the dew to Israel. In a dry land where rain was rare in summer, the heavy dew kept plants alive. Israel's love was like passing dew. God's love is like faithful dew, refreshing his people every morning.

And Israel will flourish. He shall blossom like the lily, beautiful and quick to bloom. He shall take root like the trees of Lebanon, the great cedars with deep, strong roots. Beauty and strength together.

his shoots shall spread out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.

The pictures keep coming: branches spreading wide, the lasting beauty of the olive tree, which can live for centuries, and the fragrance of Lebanon's cedar forests. The whole land that had been cursed with drought and thorns (2:12; 9:6; 10:8) is now a garden.

They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon.

They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow. In 4:13 the people worshipped idols under oak trees because their shade is good. Now they find real shade in God himself. He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty (Ps 91:1). (The ESV notes that my shadow is literally "his shadow".) And they will flourish like the grain, the vine and the wine of Lebanon. The very gifts they once sought from Baal, grain and wine, God now gives freely to those who dwell with him.

verseByVerse.quote: O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you. I am like an evergreen cypress; from me comes your fruit. Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them; for the ways of the LORD are right, and the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you. I am like an evergreen cypress; from me comes your fruit.

God asks, what have I to do with idols? The answer is: nothing. God will not share his people with idols. And he does not need to, because he is everything they need. It is I who answer and look after you. (The ESV notes that you is literally "him".) Baal never answered. God does.

Then comes a remarkable picture. I am like an evergreen cypress. It is a rare picture: God compares himself to a tree. The Baal cult used sacred trees. God says, in effect, "I am the true evergreen, always alive, never withering." And from me comes your fruit. Everything good in Israel's life would come from God.

Jesus said the same about himself: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me (John 15:4). Christian fruitfulness is never our own achievement. It comes from union with Christ.

Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them; for the ways of the LORD are right, and the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them.

The book ends with a word to the reader. Whoever is wise, let him understand these things. Hosea is not just a record of what happened long ago. It is a call to each of us to be wise.

And there are only two ways to respond. The ways of the LORD are right. The same ways, the same word, the same God, lead to two different results. The upright walk in them, and find life. Transgressors stumble in them, and fall. It is the choice of Psalm 1: the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish (Ps 1:6). Peter says the same of Christ himself: for believers he is precious, but to those who do not believe he is A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense (1 Pet 2:8).

So Hosea ends where the gospel ends. God has loved an unfaithful people with a love that will not let them go. He has paid the price to buy them back. He has promised to heal their unfaithfulness and love them freely. The question left for the wise reader is simple: will you return to the LORD your God?

14.title: I Will Love Them Freely
14.overview:
Israel is called to return to the LORD, for it has stumbled because of its iniquity. They are to take words with them and pray that God would take away all iniquity and accept what is good, so that they may offer the praise of their lips. They will renounce trust in Assyria, horses and idols, saying that in God the orphan finds mercy (vv. 1-3).

God promises to heal their apostasy and love them freely, for his anger has turned away. He will be like the dew to Israel, and they will blossom like the lily, take root like the trees of Lebanon, spread like the olive and be fragrant like Lebanon. They will return and dwell in his shade and flourish like grain and the vine (vv. 4-7).

God has nothing to do with idols; he answers and cares for Ephraim; he is like an evergreen cypress, and from him comes their fruit. The wise will understand these things, for the LORD's ways are right: the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them (vv. 8-9).
14.theology:
God calls sinners to return, and repentance begins by owning our iniquity (v. 1).

God gives the words of confession; true repentance asks God to take away all sin and offers the praise of our lips (v. 2; Heb 13:15).

Repentance renounces every false savior, and helpless sinners find mercy in God (v. 3; 1:6).

God heals the wandering heart and loves his people freely, turning his anger away, as he does in Christ (v. 4; Titus 3:4-5).

God's faithful love makes his people flourish, and their fruit comes from union with him (vv. 5-8; Ps 91:1; John 15:4).

The ways of the LORD are right; the wise walk in them, but transgressors stumble (v. 9; Ps 1:6; 1 Pet 2:7-8).
14.examples:
A people who bring words instead of more sacrifices.

Three false saviors given up: alliances, armies and idols.

An orphan who finds mercy.

"I will love them freely."

Dew that does not go away.

A dry land turned into a garden of lilies, cedars and olives.

God himself as an evergreen tree.
